pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is the trough (pre-dose) level, rather than the peak, the key monitoring level in once-daily gentamicin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Efficacy comes from a high peak, but toxicity relates to sustained drug exposure. A high trough shows the drug has not cleared before the next dose (accumulation), which drives nephro- and ototoxicity — so the trough guides dose adjustment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Apart from drug levels, what should be monitored in a patient on an aminoglycoside?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Renal function (U&Es) to detect nephrotoxicity, and symptoms of ototoxicity — ask about hearing loss, balance problems and tinnitus.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which co-prescribed drugs increase the risk of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Other nephrotoxins add to the risk: vancomycin, ciclosporin, amphotericin, iodinated contrast, and NSAIDs. Combine cautiously and monitor renal function closely.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drug class notably worsens aminoglycoside ototoxicity, and which class do aminoglycosides potentiate?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) add to ototoxicity. Aminoglycosides potentiate non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers, prolonging paralysis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do glycopeptides like vancomycin work at a molecular level?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of cell-wall precursors, sterically blocking peptidoglycan synthesis (both transglycosylation and transpeptidation). This makes them slowly bactericidal. Note they bind the substrate itself, unlike beta-lactams which inhibit the enzyme (PBP).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are glycopeptides such as vancomycin effective against Gram-positive bacteria but useless against Gram-negatives?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are large molecules that cannot cross the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria to reach the cell wall. Their spectrum is therefore Gram-positives only.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient has a serious MRSA bacteraemia. Which IV antibiotic is a standard first choice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: IV vancomycin. It is a mainstay for MRSA and serious Gram-positive infections including bacteraemia, endocarditis and osteomyelitis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Name the main clinical indications for IV vancomycin.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: MRSA and serious Gram-positive infections (bacteraemia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis; cellulitis in penicillin-allergic patients), coagulase-negative staph line infections, and empirical cover in neutropenic or line sepsis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is a patient with cellulitis and a documented penicillin allergy a candidate for vancomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Vancomycin is a non-beta-lactam Gram-positive agent, so it provides cover against staphylococci and streptococci without the cross-reactivity risk of penicillins in a penicillin-allergic patient.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line antibiotic for Clostridioides difficile infection under current NICE guidance, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oral vancomycin, 125 mg four times daily for 10 days (500 mg QDS in severe/complicated disease). It has superseded metronidazole as first-line.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why does ORAL vancomycin work for C. difficile when IV vancomycin does not?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed from the gut, so it stays in the bowel lumen and reaches high concentrations at the site of infection. IV vancomycin does not achieve adequate luminal levels, so it does not treat C. difficile.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Can oral vancomycin be used to treat a systemic Gram-positive infection such as MRSA bacteraemia?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. Oral vancomycin is not absorbed from the gut, so it cannot reach the bloodstream or tissues. Systemic infection requires the IV route; the oral form is only for C. difficile in the bowel.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: For C. difficile, what are the second-line and multiply-recurrent treatment options after oral vancomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Fidaxomicin is second-line (and for a first recurrence). Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) is used for multiply-recurrent infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on IV vancomycin develops a rising creatinine. What is the most important toxicity to consider, and what worsens it?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nephrotoxicity/AKI, which is dose- and level-related. Risk is increased when combined with piperacillin-tazobactam (MHRA warning) and is worse with concurrent gentamicin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which combination with vancomycin carries an MHRA-flagged increased risk of acute kidney injury?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam. This combination carries a recognised (MHRA) signal of increased AKI risk, so renal function should be monitored closely.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient develops flushing, a rash on the upper body and hypotension shortly after starting a vancomycin infusion. What is this and how do you manage it?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Red man (red person) syndrome: a non-allergic histamine release caused by rapid infusion. It is NOT a true allergy, so vancomycin can be continued by simply slowing the infusion rate.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Is red man syndrome an allergy to vancomycin, and does it mean the drug must be stopped permanently?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. It is a rate-related histamine reaction, not an IgE-mediated allergy. Vancomycin can be continued at a slower infusion rate rather than being abandoned.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides nephrotoxicity and red man syndrome, list other important adverse effects of vancomycin.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ototoxicity (less than aminoglycosides), severe cutaneous reactions (DRESS/SJS/TEN -> stop the drug), thrombophlebitis at the infusion site, and neutropenia/thrombocytopenia on prolonged courses.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How should IV vancomycin be infused to avoid red man syndrome?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Give it slowly, over at least 60 minutes (and no faster than 10 mg/min, whichever is longer). Rapid infusion triggers the histamine reaction.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How is IV vancomycin dosed and monitored to hit therapeutic targets?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Give a loading dose (25-30 mg/kg) then dose to target levels using AUC-guidance or trough concentrations, with higher targets (trough 15-20 mg/L) for serious MRSA infections like endocarditis, bacteraemia and osteomyelitis. Monitor levels plus U&Es/renal function, and FBC on prolonged courses.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What routine safety monitoring is essential for a patient on IV vancomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Serum vancomycin levels (trough or AUC) to keep within target, and U&Es/renal function to detect nephrotoxicity. Check FBC on prolonged courses for neutropenia/thrombocytopenia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What does VRE stand for, and why does it matter for vancomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci. These organisms have remodelled cell-wall precursors that vancomycin can no longer bind effectively, so vancomycin fails and an alternative agent is needed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drugs increase the risk of toxicity when co-prescribed with vancomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Agents with additive nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity: aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin), piperacillin-tazobactam, loop diuretics, amphotericin, ciclosporin, and IV contrast.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does teicoplanin compare with vancomycin in mechanism and spectrum?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Teicoplanin is a glycopeptide with the same D-Ala-D-Ala cell-wall mechanism and the same Gram-positive/MRSA cover as vancomycin. The key differences are practical: a long half-life and better tolerability.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is teicoplanin well suited to OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It has a long half-life allowing once-daily dosing after loading, and can be given IV OR IM. This convenient regimen makes it ideal for outpatient parenteral therapy of Gram-positive/MRSA infections such as endocarditis and bone/joint infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does teicoplanin's side-effect profile differ from vancomycin's?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Teicoplanin is generally better tolerated: less nephrotoxicity and no red man syndrome on injection. It can still cause hypersensitivity/rash and, rarely, ototoxicity or blood dyscrasias. Monitor renal function, and trough levels for deep-seated infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of metronidazole, and why is it active only against anaerobes and protozoa?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Its nitro group is reduced by low-redox carriers (ferredoxin/PFOR) present only in anaerobes and protozoa, generating a nitro radical anion that causes DNA strand breaks -> concentration-dependent bactericidal killing. Aerobic bacteria lack this low-potential reduction system, so metronidazole has no useful activity against them.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Name the main clinical uses of metronidazole.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Anaerobic infections (intra-abdominal and pelvic sepsis, aspiration pneumonia, dental/oral infections), C. difficile (now reserved/third-line, only if oral vancomycin and fidaxomicin are unsuitable), bacterial vaginosis, Trichomonas, Giardia, amoebiasis, and as part of H. pylori eradication regimens.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on metronidazole drinks alcohol and develops flushing, vomiting and tachycardia. What has happened and how is it avoided?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: This is the disulfiram-like reaction between metronidazole and alcohol. Counsel the patient to avoid all alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours after the last dose.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What side effect can develop with prolonged courses of metronidazole, and what other common adverse effect should patients be warned about?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Prolonged use can cause a peripheral neuropathy, so watch for it on long courses. A metallic taste is a common, benign side effect; other effects include GI upset and furry tongue, with rare encephalopathy/seizures.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which important anticoagulant interaction must you remember with metronidazole?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Metronidazole potentiates warfarin, raising the INR and increasing bleeding risk. It can also raise lithium and phenytoin levels.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of trimethoprim?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking folate recycling (DHF -> THF) and impairing DNA synthesis -> bacteriostatic. This folate antagonism underlies both its efficacy and its toxicities.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line indication for trimethoprim, and when is it preferred?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Uncomplicated lower UTI (200 mg BD for 3 days), used first-line only where local resistance risk is low (otherwise nitrofurantoin is preferred, as community resistance is now around 30-40%). Also used for UTI prophylaxis (100 mg nocte).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should trimethoprim be avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy, and what is the alternative?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and is teratogenic in early pregnancy, increasing the risk of neural tube defects. Use nitrofurantoin instead in early/mid pregnancy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: An elderly patient on ramipril is started on trimethoprim. What two blood abnormalities can trimethoprim cause, and why does this combination matter?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Trimethoprim blocks the renal ENaC channel (like amiloride), causing hyperkalaemia and a rise in creatinine (partly a benign competition for tubular secretion). Combined with an ACEi/ARB/spironolactone, especially in the elderly, it can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia and AKI (MHRA warning) -> check U&Es and consider withholding the RAAS drug.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must trimethoprim be avoided with methotrexate?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Both are folate antagonists, so combining them causes additive anti-folate and bone-marrow toxicity -> avoid. Trimethoprim can also raise the INR with warfarin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is co-trimoxazole, and how do its two components work together?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Co-trimoxazole is trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole. Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (competing with PABA) and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, giving sequential (dual) folate blockade -> synergistic and bactericidal.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the key indication for co-trimoxazole?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) treatment and prophylaxis, particularly in HIV/immunosuppression. It is also used for toxoplasmosis, Nocardia, some resistant UTIs, and certain MRSA/Stenotrophomonas infections.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What serious skin reaction is associated with co-trimoxazole, and what advice should patients be given?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (a sulfonamide effect). Counsel patients that if a rash develops they should stop the drug and seek medical help urgently.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: List the main contraindications/cautions for co-trimoxazole.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Sulfonamide allergy, pregnancy (folate antagonism), G6PD deficiency (haemolysis), concurrent methotrexate (fatal marrow suppression), severe hepatic/renal impairment, and blood dyscrasias.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides skin reactions, what other adverse effects and monitoring apply to co-trimoxazole?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hyperkalaemia (from trimethoprim), bone-marrow suppression, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, raised creatinine and hepatitis. Monitor FBC, U&Es (K+) and LFTs during treatment courses. It also potentiates sulfonylureas -> hypoglycaemia, and raises the INR with warfarin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does nitrofurantoin work, and why does this limit where it can be used?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is concentrated in urine, where bacterial nitroreductase activates it to reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA, ribosomes and enzymes -> bactericidal locally. Because it reaches effective levels only in the urinary tract (no systemic tissue levels), it treats lower UTI but NOT pyelonephritis or any systemic infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line indication for nitrofurantoin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Uncomplicated lower UTI (100 mg MR BD, or 50 mg QDS, for 3-7 days), including in early/mid pregnancy where trimethoprim is contraindicated (but avoid at term).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must nitrofurantoin be avoided in significant renal impairment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: With low eGFR it is both ineffective (insufficient urinary concentration) and toxic. Avoid if eGFR < 30 mL/min; eGFR 30-44 may be used with caution as a short 3-7 day course for resistant lower UTI only if there is no alternative.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When in pregnancy must nitrofurantoin be avoided, and which enzyme deficiency is also a contraindication?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Avoid at term / near delivery (36+ weeks) and in neonates because of the risk of neonatal haemolysis. Also avoid in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What toxicities can occur with long-term nitrofurantoin, and what harmless effect should patients be warned about?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Long-term use can cause chronic pulmonary fibrosis (as well as acute pulmonary reactions with fever, cough and eosinophilia), hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy -> monitor LFTs and for pulmonary/neurological symptoms on prophylaxis. It also harmlessly colours the urine brown/orange.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of clindamycin, and what are its key strengths?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit (macrolide site), inhibiting protein synthesis -> bacteriostatic. It has good Gram-positive and anaerobe cover, excellent tissue and bone penetration, and switches off toxin production in toxin-mediated disease.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the main clinical uses of clindamycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cellulitis and skin/soft-tissue infections (including in penicillin-allergic patients), necrotising fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome (added to suppress toxin production), osteomyelitis and septic arthritis (bone penetration), and dental and aspiration infections.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is clindamycin added in necrotising fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Because it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, it switches off exotoxin production in these toxin-mediated diseases, so it is added alongside other agents rather than used for its killing effect alone.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the key exam-relevant adverse effect of clindamycin, and how do you act on it?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Clindamycin is one of the highest-risk antibiotics for C. difficile colitis (the classic culprit). If a patient develops diarrhoea, stop the drug and test for C. difficile.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What contraindication and drug interaction should you note with clindamycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Avoid in anyone with previous clindamycin-associated colitis, and use caution with any history of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. It also potentiates neuromuscular blocking agents (enhanced blockade); other effects include hepatotoxicity and oesophagitis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What class of antibiotic is linezolid, and how does it work?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: An oxazolidinone. It binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks assembly of the initiation complex, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic against staphylococci and enterococci).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which resistant organisms does linezolid cover, and why is its oral formulation so useful?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It covers MRSA and VRE. It has essentially 100% oral bioavailability (oral dose = IV dose), making it a valuable oral option for MRSA/VRE and for resistant Gram-positive skin/soft-tissue and hospital pneumonia when glycopeptides fail or are unsuitable.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on long-term linezolid develops bruising and a falling platelet count. What is happening and how is it monitored?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Linezolid causes reversible myelosuppression/thrombocytopenia, typically on courses longer than 2 weeks. Monitor FBC (platelets) weekly, especially beyond 2 weeks, and limit courses to a maximum of 28 days.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must linezolid not be co-prescribed with an SSRI, and what can result?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Linezolid is a weak, reversible non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor. Combined with SSRIs/SNRIs (or triptans, pethidine) it can precipitate serotonin syndrome, so serotonergic drugs should be avoided/stopped.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Beyond serotonin syndrome, what other neurological and dietary risks come with prolonged linezolid use?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Prolonged use can cause peripheral and optic neuropathy (report visual symptoms immediately for urgent ophthalmology review) and lactic acidosis. As a weak MAOI it can also cause a hypertensive (pressor) reaction with tyramine-rich foods such as mature cheese, which should be avoided.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What class is daptomycin and how does it kill bacteria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A cyclic lipopeptide. It inserts into the Gram-positive cell membrane and depolarises it, producing rapid bactericidal killing. It covers MRSA and VRE.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the main indications for daptomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: MRSA/Gram-positive bacteraemia, right-sided endocarditis, and complicated skin/soft-tissue infection. It is used as a vancomycin alternative.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must daptomycin never be used to treat pneumonia?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Daptomycin is inactivated by lung surfactant, so it is ineffective in the lungs and must not be used for respiratory-tract infection/pneumonia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on daptomycin develops muscle pain. What toxicity should you check for, and how is it monitored?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Daptomycin can cause a myopathy with raised creatine kinase (CK), risking rhabdomyolysis. Monitor CK weekly and watch for muscle pain.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What should be done about a patient's statin when starting daptomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Statins add to daptomycin's myotoxicity, so they should be stopped/held during daptomycin treatment to avoid additive myopathy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does rifampicin work, and why is it never given alone for active TB?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking transcription (bactericidal). It is never used as monotherapy because single point mutations cause rapid resistance, so it is always given in combination.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the key clinical uses of rifampicin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Tuberculosis (the 'R' of RIPE, always in combination), meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae prophylaxis for close contacts, and prosthetic-material/biofilm infections (added to another agent). Also used as an adjunct in some staph infections and in leprosy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill is started on rifampicin. What advice must she be given and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer that speeds up breakdown of many drugs, reducing the contraceptive's effectiveness. She should use an additional or non-hormonal method of contraception.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which important drugs have their effect reduced by rifampicin's enzyme induction?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin lowers levels/effect of hormonal contraceptives, warfarin (falling INR), DOACs, corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin/tacrolimus, among others. Doses may need adjusting and warfarin needs closer monitoring.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on rifampicin is alarmed that his urine and tears have turned orange-red. What do you tell him?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: This is a harmless, expected effect of rifampicin, which discolours urine, tears and sweat orange-red. Warn that it can permanently stain soft contact lenses.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What organ toxicity requires monitoring during rifampicin therapy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hepatotoxicity (raised transaminases). Check LFTs at baseline and during treatment; avoid in significant hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the standard regimen of fosfomycin for an uncomplicated lower UTI?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A single oral 3 g sachet. Its convenient one-off dose makes it a useful option when other oral agents are unsuitable.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When is fosfomycin a particularly valuable choice for a urinary infection?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: For lower UTI caused by resistant organisms, including many ESBL-producing Gram-negatives, where other oral options are limited.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does fosfomycin work, and in whom should it be avoided?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It blocks the first step of bacterial cell-wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis, making it bactericidal. Avoid in severe renal impairment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is colistin (a polymyxin), and when is it used?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A last-resort/last-line antibiotic for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, such as carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter or Klebsiella. It is a reserved, specialist agent.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does colistin kill Gram-negative bacteria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It disrupts the Gram-negative outer membrane, acting as a cationic detergent that binds the lipopolysaccharide and destabilises the membrane, giving bactericidal killing.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the two dose-limiting toxicities that restrict colistin to reserved use?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting) and neurotoxicity (paraesthesiae, neuromuscular blockade). Monitor renal function closely and watch for neurological symptoms; this is why it is a reserved, specialist agent.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How can colistin be given in cystic fibrosis, and what caution applies in myasthenia gravis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It can be nebulised for chronic Pseudomonas infection in cystic fibrosis. Avoid in myasthenia gravis because it potentiates neuromuscular blockade.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which co-prescribed drugs increase the risk of colistin nephrotoxicity?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Other nephrotoxic drugs add to the risk, including aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin, NSAIDs and loop diuretics. Renal function should be monitored closely.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What four drugs make up standard first-line therapy for active TB (the RIPE regimen)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol. All four are given for the first 2 months (intensive phase), then rifampicin + isoniazid are continued for a further 4 months = 6 months total.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In the 6-month RIPE regimen, which drugs run the whole 6 months and which only the first 2 months?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin and isoniazid run all 6 months. Pyrazinamide and ethambutol are given only during the first 2-month intensive phase.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does treatment differ for TB meningitis / CNS TB compared with pulmonary TB?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: CNS TB is treated for 12 months (rather than 6) and adjunctive corticosteroids are added.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How is latent TB treated?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Either 3 months of isoniazid + rifampicin (3HR), or 6 months of isoniazid alone (6H). Pyridoxine is co-prescribed with the isoniazid.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must active TB never be treated with a single drug?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Monotherapy rapidly selects for resistant bacilli. Multiple drugs are combined to prevent resistance. Rifampicin resistance in particular defines multi-drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), which needs specialist regimens.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Is TB a notifiable disease, and what does that mean in practice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Yes. TB must be notified to public health on suspicion (not just on confirmation), triggering contact tracing. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is used for at-risk patients to ensure adherence.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which three of the four RIPE drugs share hepatotoxicity, and what baseline test does this mandate?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide are all hepatotoxic. Check baseline LFTs before starting, and counsel every patient to report jaundice, nausea or malaise and stop the drugs.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides LFTs, what baseline screening should be done before starting TB treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: An HIV test and hepatitis B and C serology, in addition to baseline LFTs and renal function.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which of the four TB drugs is the most hepatotoxic?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic of the four.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the simple mechanism of action of rifampicin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It blocks bacterial RNA polymerase, stopping transcription. This is bactericidal, with a useful sterilising action on semi-dormant bacilli.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on rifampicin is alarmed that their urine and tears have turned orange-red. What do you tell them?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: This is a harmless, expected effect - rifampicin colours the urine, tears and sweat orange-red. Warn them it can permanently stain soft contact lenses.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer. What effect does this have on other drugs?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: By inducing metabolising enzymes it speeds up clearance and reduces the effect of many drugs - the combined pill and POP, warfarin, DOACs, corticosteroids and ciclosporin/tacrolimus.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill is started on rifampicin. What contraceptive advice is essential?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer and reduces the efficacy of the pill (and POP), risking unintended pregnancy. Advise additional or non-hormonal contraception.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does rifampicin affect a patient taking warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: As an enzyme inducer it increases warfarin metabolism, so the INR falls and the anticoagulant effect is reduced - the dose usually needs to be increased with close INR monitoring.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the simple mechanism of action of isoniazid?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It blocks mycolic acid synthesis, disrupting the mycobacterial cell wall. This is bactericidal.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the classic neurological side effect of isoniazid, and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Peripheral neuropathy, caused by vitamin B6 depletion. Co-prescribe pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to prevent it.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which patients on isoniazid are at highest risk of peripheral neuropathy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Those with diabetes, alcohol excess, HIV, malnutrition, renal impairment, pregnancy, and the elderly. Pyridoxine is especially important in these groups.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides hepatotoxicity and neuropathy, what autoimmune-type side effect can isoniazid cause?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A drug-induced lupus (SLE-like) syndrome.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Isoniazid is an enzyme inhibitor - the opposite of rifampicin. What is the clinical consequence?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: By inhibiting metabolising enzymes it slows clearance and raises the levels of other drugs, e.g. phenytoin and carbamazepine, risking toxicity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: For how long is pyrazinamide given, and why not longer?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Only during the first 2 months (the intensive phase). Its sterilising action on intracellular bacilli allows the overall regimen to be shortened to 6 months; it is then stopped.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What metabolic side effect of pyrazinamide can precipitate acute gout?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia by reducing urate excretion, which can trigger an acute gout attack. Avoid pyrazinamide in patients with acute gout.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on pyrazinamide develops joint pain but has a normal urate and no gout. What is this and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A non-gouty arthralgia, which is not urate-related. It is treated with simple analgesia, not urate-lowering drugs, and does not usually require stopping the drug.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: For how long is ethambutol given in standard TB treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Only during the first 2-month intensive phase, mainly to cover possible drug resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the classic sight-threatening toxicity of ethambutol?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Optic neuritis, presenting as reduced visual acuity and red-green colour blindness. It is usually reversible if the drug is stopped early.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What monitoring and counselling are required for a patient starting ethambutol?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Check visual acuity and colour vision at baseline (and periodically). Warn the patient to report any change in vision immediately and stop the drug.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why does ethambutol need dose adjustment in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is renally excreted, so in renal impairment it accumulates, and this accumulation raises the risk of optic neuritis. Reduce the dose and monitor accordingly.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which single RIPE drug is bactericidal by blocking bacterial RNA polymerase, and is a potent enzyme inducer causing orange secretions?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin - it blocks RNA polymerase (bactericidal), turns body fluids orange-red, and as an enzyme inducer weakens the pill, warfarin, steroids and transplant drugs.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole) work, and are they fungistatic or fungicidal?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They block ergosterol synthesis (inhibiting fungal 14-alpha-demethylase), damaging the fungal cell membrane. They are fungistatic against Candida but fungicidal against Aspergillus/moulds.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which azole is used for Candida (thrush) and cryptococcal meningitis, and why is it good for the latter?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Fluconazole. It has good CSF penetration, so it is used for cryptococcal meningitis (as consolidation/maintenance after amphotericin + flucytosine induction). It covers Candida and cryptococcus but has NO Aspergillus cover.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient has invasive candidiasis and is being stepped down from IV therapy to an oral azole. Which one?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Fluconazole. Echinocandins are first-line for invasive candidiasis/candidaemia, then step down to oral fluconazole once the patient is stable and the organism is susceptible.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line azole for invasive aspergillosis, and what monitoring does it need?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Voriconazole. It requires mandatory therapeutic drug monitoring (unpredictable drug levels). Fluconazole does NOT cover Aspergillus.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What characteristic side effects does voriconazole cause?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Visual disturbances and hallucinations, and phototoxicity that raises the risk of skin cancer (squamous cell carcinoma) — patients must avoid sun exposure and use sun protection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which azoles have the broadest spectrum (including moulds), and which one is unusual for its QT effect?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Posaconazole and isavuconazole — broadest cover including moulds, and used as salvage/second-line for mucormycosis (first-line is amphotericin + surgery). Uniquely, isavuconazole SHORTENS the QT interval (the exception to the class, which prolongs QT).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the three big class-wide safety themes of the azoles?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: 1) Hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs). 2) QT prolongation. 3) Potent inhibition of the metabolism of other drugs, raising their levels (e.g. statins, warfarin, tacrolimus).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is simvastatin contraindicated with an azole, and what should be done with warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Azoles inhibit the metabolism of other drugs, raising their levels. This causes dangerously high simvastatin levels and rhabdomyolysis (so simvastatin is contraindicated). Warfarin levels rise too, increasing the INR and bleeding risk — monitor INR and reduce the warfarin dose.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: An azole raises the levels of tacrolimus/ciclosporin and of sulfonylureas — what are the consequences?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: By inhibiting their metabolism, azoles raise tacrolimus/ciclosporin levels (toxicity — monitor levels) and raise sulfonylurea levels, causing hypoglycaemia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A pregnant woman has vaginal thrush. Why avoid oral fluconazole, and what should you use instead?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Avoid oral azoles in pregnancy — even a single 150 mg fluconazole dose is linked to miscarriage (MHRA). Use topical clotrimazole instead.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is itraconazole contraindicated in heart failure?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Itraconazole is a negative inotrope, so it can precipitate or worsen heart failure (MHRA warning).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must itraconazole capsules be taken with food, and what reduces their absorption?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Itraconazole capsules need stomach acid to be absorbed, so take with food. PPIs and antacids reduce their absorption. (The oral solution does not have this problem.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does amphotericin B work and what is its spectrum?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is a polyene that binds fungal ergosterol, forming pores in the membrane that cause leakage and cell death. It is fungicidal and the broadest-spectrum antifungal.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When is amphotericin B used?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: For severe/invasive fungal infection — invasive candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis induction (with flucytosine), invasive aspergillosis, and mucormycosis (with surgery). Often first-line for life-threatening fungal infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the dose-limiting toxicity of amphotericin B and its electrolyte effects?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nephrotoxicity is dose-limiting — it reduces renal function and causes potassium and magnesium wasting (hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia). Monitor U&Es (K+, Mg2+) and renal function, and supplement electrolytes.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the 'shake and bake' reaction with amphotericin B?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: An infusion reaction — fever, rigors, and hypotension during the infusion. Pre-medicate/pre-hydrate to reduce it.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which amphotericin B formulation is preferred and why must you prescribe it by brand?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The liposomal formulation is preferred because it is much less nephrotoxic. Formulations (conventional vs liposomal vs lipid-complex) are NOT interchangeable and have very different doses — always prescribe by brand and verify the dose, as dosing errors have been fatal (MHRA).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) work, and why are they so well tolerated?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They block the fungal cell wall by inhibiting beta-glucan synthase. This target is absent in human cells, so they are very well tolerated with few drug interactions.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line treatment for invasive candidiasis/candidaemia, and what do you step down to?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: An echinocandin (e.g. caspofungin, micafungin or anidulafungin) is first-line, including in critically ill or possibly azole-resistant patients. Step down to oral fluconazole once the patient is stable and the organism is susceptible.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should echinocandins NOT be used for fungal meningitis or a fungal UTI?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Echinocandins have no CNS or urinary penetration, so they do not reach therapeutic levels in the brain/CSF or urine.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How is the echinocandin caspofungin administered?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: IV only — a loading dose then once daily. (Micafungin and anidulafungin are also given once daily IV.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does terbinafine work and where does it concentrate?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is an allylamine that blocks ergosterol synthesis (inhibiting squalene epoxidase), which is fungicidal against dermatophytes. It concentrates in skin, nails and hair.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line oral agent for fungal nail infection (onychomycosis)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oral terbinafine. It is also first-line oral treatment for dermatophyte infections and tinea capitis (especially Trichophyton).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the typical oral terbinafine course length for fingernail versus toenail infection?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Terbinafine 250 mg once daily — 6 weeks for fingernails and 12 weeks (3 months) for toenails, reflecting the slower growth of toenails.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the key side effects and monitoring for oral terbinafine?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hepatotoxicity — check LFTs before and during treatment and stop if deranged. A characteristic taste/smell disturbance that may be prolonged or even permanent. It can also cause mood change (depression/anxiety).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does nystatin work and why does it act only locally?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nystatin is a polyene (like amphotericin) that binds ergosterol to form membrane pores. It is NOT absorbed from the gut, so it acts purely topically on mucosal surfaces with no systemic effect.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is nystatin used for and how is it given for oral thrush?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oral/oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) and topical candidal infections. Given as a swish-and-swallow oral suspension held in the mouth, continued for about 48 hours after symptoms resolve. Because it is not absorbed, it has no systemic effect and no clinically significant interactions.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does griseofulvin work?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It disrupts fungal microtubules/the mitotic spindle to inhibit fungal mitosis, and it deposits in keratin (skin, hair and nails).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is griseofulvin's main indication today?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It remains licensed first-line for tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) in children, especially Microsporum species. It is largely replaced by terbinafine otherwise (terbinafine is preferred for Trichophyton).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must griseofulvin be avoided in pregnancy, and what precaution applies to men?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy. Women need effective contraception during treatment and for 1 month after; men should avoid fathering a child for 6 months after treatment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Griseofulvin is an enzyme inducer — what practical consequences does this have?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: As an enzyme inducer it reduces the effectiveness of the hormonal contraceptive pill (an additional contraceptive method is needed) and reduces warfarin efficacy. It also has a disulfiram-like interaction with alcohol.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does aciclovir achieve its selectivity for virus-infected cells?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Aciclovir is a guanosine analogue that must be monophosphorylated by VIRAL thymidine kinase before host kinases add the remaining phosphates. Only infected cells carry this viral enzyme, so the active drug is generated almost exclusively where the virus is.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Once activated, how does aciclovir triphosphate stop viral replication?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and, lacking a 3'-OH group, terminates the growing DNA chain -> replication halts.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which viruses does aciclovir treat?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Herpes simplex (HSV) -> genital herpes, herpes encephalitis, herpetic keratitis; and varicella-zoster (VZV) -> chickenpox in at-risk adults and shingles (especially ophthalmic/severe).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient presents with fever, confusion and seizures, and HSV encephalitis is suspected. What is the immediate treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: IV aciclovir, started empirically without delay - HSV encephalitis is a medical emergency. Typical regimen is IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 14-21 days; do not wait for confirmation before starting.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the main toxicity of IV aciclovir and how do you prevent it?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Crystal nephropathy -> crystalluria and AKI, especially if the patient is dehydrated. Prevent it by keeping the patient well hydrated and infusing the drug slowly; dose-adjust in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides nephrotoxicity, what side effect of aciclovir is seen particularly in renal impairment or at high dose?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Neurotoxicity - confusion and other CNS disturbance. It is more likely with renal impairment or high doses, so reduce the dose accordingly.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is valaciclovir and why is it used instead of aciclovir?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Valaciclovir is the oral prodrug of aciclovir. It is much better absorbed, so it allows effective treatment with fewer daily doses (e.g. 500 mg-1 g rather than aciclovir 400-800 mg five times a day).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which antiviral is the treatment of choice for cytomegalovirus (CMV) disease?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ganciclovir (or its oral prodrug valganciclovir). It is used for CMV retinitis in AIDS, CMV pneumonitis/colitis, and CMV prophylaxis/treatment in transplant recipients.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the dose-limiting toxicity of ganciclovir, and what must you monitor?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Bone-marrow suppression - neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia. Monitor the FBC; interrupt therapy if the neutrophil or platelet count falls too low.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Contrast the headline toxicity of ganciclovir with that of aciclovir.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ganciclovir -> bone-marrow suppression (monitor FBC), whereas aciclovir -> crystal nephropathy/AKI (keep hydrated). Both are guanosine analogues but their dose-limiting toxicities differ.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should ganciclovir be handled as a cytotoxic drug, and what advice applies in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is teratogenic, carcinogenic and impairs fertility, so it is handled with cytotoxic precautions. It is avoided in pregnancy; effective contraception is needed, including barrier contraception for men for 90 days after treatment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do oseltamivir and zanamivir work against influenza?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are neuraminidase (sialidase) inhibitors. Blocking neuraminidase stops newly formed virions detaching from the host cell, so release and spread of new influenza virus is prevented.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Within what time window must influenza antivirals be started to be most effective?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Within 48 hours of symptom onset - oseltamivir and zanamivir are most useful when started early.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the two main uses of oseltamivir/zanamivir in influenza, and in whom?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis of influenza, used mainly in at-risk groups such as the elderly, pregnant women, those with chronic disease, and the immunocompromised.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How are oseltamivir and zanamivir given, and what caution applies to zanamivir?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oseltamivir is oral (75 mg twice daily for treatment); zanamivir is inhaled. Zanamivir can cause bronchospasm, so use it with caution in asthma and COPD.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What neuropsychiatric safety point applies to influenza antivirals, and in whom?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rare neuropsychiatric events (confusion, abnormal behaviour, self-harm) have been reported, particularly in children and adolescents. Monitor for abnormal behaviour in this group.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of the NRTI class (e.g. tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, zidovudine)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors. After intracellular phosphorylation to the triphosphate, they lack a 3'-OH group and so chain-terminate HIV reverse transcriptase, blocking viral DNA synthesis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is meant by the NRTI 'backbone' of ART?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Standard HIV treatment combines two NRTIs (the 'backbone') plus a third agent from another class. This combination approach suppresses the virus and limits resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What does 'U=U' mean and why is it the goal of ART?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Undetectable = Untransmittable. The aim of ART is durable suppression to an undetectable viral load; a person with an undetectable load cannot transmit HIV sexually.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drug combination is the standard HIV PrEP, and how can it be taken?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Tenofovir (TDF)/emtricitabine ('Truvada'). It is taken either daily or event-based (2-1-1 dosing) and is available through sexual health services; it is also used for PEP.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the key toxicities of tenofovir (TDF), and how are they mitigated?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Renal impairment (proximal tubulopathy/Fanconi) and reduced bone mineral density. Monitor renal function and bone health; the newer TAF formulation is safer for kidneys and bone.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which characteristic side effect is associated with zidovudine?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Anaemia and macrocytosis (plus GI upset). Monitor the FBC in patients on zidovudine.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What serious metabolic complication is linked to the older NRTIs?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Lactic acidosis (e.g. with zidovudine, didanosine), arising from off-target inhibition of mitochondrial function.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must you check hepatitis B status before starting or stopping tenofovir, lamivudine or emtricitabine?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: These NRTIs are also active against hepatitis B. Stopping them in a co-infected patient can trigger a hepatitis B flare, so HBV status must be known before starting and before stopping.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What test is mandatory before prescribing abacavir, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: HLA-B*5701 testing. A positive result predicts a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction, so abacavir is avoided in those who carry it.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do NNRTIs (e.g. efavirenz, rilpivirine, nevirapine) inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind an allosteric pocket on the enzyme, causing non-competitive inhibition. Unlike NRTIs they need no intracellular phosphorylation. They are used as a 'third agent' with an NRTI backbone, though integrase inhibitors are now often preferred first-line.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why does the NNRTI class have a 'low genetic barrier to resistance'?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A single point mutation can confer resistance to the whole class, so viral resistance emerges easily if adherence is poor or the drug is used alone.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the characteristic side effects of efavirenz and how is dosing timed to help?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: CNS/neuropsychiatric effects - vivid dreams, dizziness and mood change. Taking the dose at night means the patient sleeps through the worst of these effects. Caution in those with a psychiatric history.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What two serious toxicities characterise nevirapine, and how is dosing managed?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hepatotoxicity and severe rash (up to Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Nevirapine is started with a lead-in (200 mg once daily for 14 days before escalating to twice daily); do not escalate if rash or LFT rise occurs, and monitor LFTs closely early on.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Efavirenz behaves as an enzyme inducer. What is the clinical consequence for co-prescribed drugs?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: By inducing drug metabolism it lowers the levels and effectiveness of other medicines - for example reducing the reliability of the contraceptive pill, and affecting statins and methadone. Consider these interactions when co-prescribing.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must rilpivirine not be taken with a proton pump inhibitor?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rilpivirine needs gastric acid for absorption. PPIs raise gastric pH and reduce its absorption, risking treatment failure; it should be taken with food and PPIs avoided.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of the HIV protease inhibitors (PIs) such as darunavir and lopinavir?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They block HIV protease, so the virus produces immature, non-infectious virions. Used as part of combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), often in second-line/resistance regimens.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is low-dose ritonavir (or cobicistat) added to an HIV protease-inhibitor regimen?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: As a pharmacokinetic 'booster': it potently inhibits drug metabolism, raising blood levels of the active PI so it can be given once/twice daily. Ritonavir is itself a PI, but cobicistat is purely a booster with no antiviral activity of its own.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are HIV protease inhibitors (and their ritonavir/cobicistat booster) such a major drug-interaction class?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The booster potently inhibits drug metabolism, so it raises the levels of many co-prescribed drugs to potentially toxic concentrations. Always check every co-prescription before adding a boosted PI.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which two commonly prescribed drugs are contraindicated with a boosted HIV protease inhibitor?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Simvastatin (and lovastatin) and oral midazolam. The booster inhibits their metabolism, causing dangerous accumulation -> rhabdomyolysis risk with the statin, and excessive sedation/respiratory depression with midazolam. Ergot derivatives are also contraindicated.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on a boosted HIV protease inhibitor is also using inhaled/intranasal fluticasone. What is the danger?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The booster inhibits fluticasone metabolism, so systemic steroid levels rise -> iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome and adrenal suppression. Avoid this combination.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the characteristic class metabolic side effects of HIV protease inhibitors?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance/hyperglycaemia, and lipodystrophy (fat redistribution), plus GI upset/diarrhoea and deranged LFTs. Effectively a metabolic-syndrome picture.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What should be monitored in a patient taking an HIV protease inhibitor?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Lipids, glucose/HbA1c and LFTs (for the metabolic and hepatic effects), alongside viral load and CD4 count to check treatment response.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of the integrase strand-transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) such as dolutegravir and bictegravir?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They block HIV integrase, preventing viral DNA from integrating into the host cell genome. They are now the first-line 'third agent' in ART.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are INSTIs (dolutegravir, bictegravir) the preferred first-line third agent in HIV treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They give potent, rapid viral suppression, have few drug interactions and are very well tolerated. The UK favours rapid/same-day ART start, often as a single-tablet regimen.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the common side effects of the INSTIs?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Generally very well tolerated, but can cause weight gain, headache and insomnia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: An HIV patient on dolutegravir has a small rise in serum creatinine but is otherwise well. How do you interpret this?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Dolutegravir (and bictegravir) reduce tubular secretion of creatinine, so the measured creatinine rises slightly without any true fall in GFR. It is a benign effect, not kidney injury.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must INSTIs be separated in time from antacids, iron, calcium and multivitamins?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Divalent cations chelate the INSTI in the gut and drastically reduce its absorption, risking treatment failure. The doses must be spaced apart.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A diabetic patient on metformin is started on dolutegravir. What interaction must you consider?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Dolutegravir (and bictegravir) raise metformin levels, increasing the risk of side effects/lactic acidosis. Cap the metformin dose (about 1 g/day).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Is dolutegravir safe to use in pregnancy, including at conception?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Yes. The earlier neural-tube-defect signal has been reassured (very low risk), and dolutegravir is now recommended in pregnancy, including around conception.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is cabotegravir and how is it distinctive among the INSTIs?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is a long-acting injectable INSTI. It is given with rilpivirine as maintenance ART, or on its own for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of maraviroc in HIV?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is an entry inhibitor: it blocks the CCR5 co-receptor that HIV uses to enter CD4 cells, so the virus cannot get into the cell.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must a tropism test be done before prescribing maraviroc?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Maraviroc only works against CCR5-tropic virus. If the virus uses a different co-receptor the drug is ineffective, so a tropism assay must confirm CCR5-tropic virus first. It is a niche/resistance-setting agent.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the key management-changing toxicity of maraviroc?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hepatotoxicity, which may be preceded by an allergic/hypersensitivity reaction. Monitor LFTs and stop the drug immediately if hepatitis or a hypersensitivity reaction occurs.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for hepatitis C, and how are they recognised by name?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oral drugs targeting hepatitis C viral proteins, given as fixed-dose combinations: '-buvir' (e.g. sofosbuvir, a nucleotide chain-terminator), '-asvir' (e.g. ledipasvir, velpatasvir, daclatasvir) and '-previr' (e.g. glecaprevir, a protease inhibitor).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How effective are DAA combinations for chronic hepatitis C, and how are they taken?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Taken orally as fixed-dose combinations for 8-12 weeks, they achieve cure (sustained virological response) in over 95% of patients. They are well tolerated and have replaced interferon/ribavirin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which infection must you screen for before starting hepatitis C DAAs, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hepatitis B (check HBsAg/anti-HBc). There is a risk of hepatitis B reactivation during DAA treatment for hepatitis C, so it must be identified and managed beforehand.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should sofosbuvir not be combined with amiodarone?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The combination can cause severe, potentially life-threatening bradycardia. Avoid co-prescribing them.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which hepatitis C DAA regimens should be avoided in decompensated (Child-Pugh B/C) liver disease?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Protease-inhibitor-containing ('-previr') regimens are avoided in decompensated liver disease.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism and role of entecavir and tenofovir in chronic hepatitis B?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are oral nucleos(t)ide analogues that inhibit HBV replication. They are first-line to suppress viral load and reduce the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, and to prevent reactivation during immunosuppression/chemotherapy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Do entecavir and tenofovir cure hepatitis B?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. They suppress HBV replication but rarely cure it, because the viral cccDNA reservoir persists in the nucleus. Treatment is therefore often long-term or indefinite. They do have a high barrier to resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must hepatitis B nucleos(t)ide therapy (entecavir/tenofovir) not be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Stopping can trigger a hepatitis flare and even hepatic decompensation as viral replication rebounds. Therapy should not be discontinued abruptly.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the notable toxicities of tenofovir, and what monitoring do they require?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Renal impairment and reduced bone density (the TAF formulation is safer). Monitor renal function; nephrotoxicity is additive with NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins. Also monitor HBV DNA/viral load and LFTs.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How should entecavir be taken to ensure adequate absorption?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: On an empty stomach (food reduces its absorption).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine kill malaria parasites?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They concentrate in the parasite's acidic food vacuole and block haem detoxification (they inhibit conversion of toxic free haem into inert haemozoin). The build-up of toxic free haem kills blood-stage plasmodia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: For which type of malaria is chloroquine the blood-stage treatment of choice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Confirmed NON-falciparum malaria (P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi). It is rarely used for falciparum because of widespread resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: After chloroquine treats P. vivax or P. ovale malaria, what additional drug is needed and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Primaquine, for radical cure. It clears the dormant liver (hypnozoite) stages of vivax and ovale to prevent relapse; chloroquine only kills the blood stage.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is now the most common clinical use of hydroxychloroquine?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: As a DMARD (immunomodulator) in SLE and rheumatoid arthritis, rather than as an antimalarial.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the key long-term toxicity of hydroxychloroquine and how does it appear?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Retinopathy - an irreversible 'bull's-eye' maculopathy - with prolonged use. It is why patients need retinal screening.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What eye monitoring is required for patients on long-term hydroxychloroquine?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A baseline retinal assessment, then annual OCT retinal screening, usually starting after 5 years of treatment (earlier if higher dose, renal impairment, or on tamoxifen).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides retinopathy, name two cardiac adverse effects of chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: QT prolongation and cardiomyopathy / conduction disorders (which can be fatal or irreversible).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is chloroquine dangerous in a household with small children?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is highly toxic in overdose - just 1-2 adult tablets can kill a small child. It also lowers the seizure threshold.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which antimalarial should be used with caution in a patient with epilepsy, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, because they lower the seizure threshold. (Mefloquine is similarly avoided with any seizure history.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do artemisinins (e.g. artemether, artesunate) kill malaria parasites?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Parasite haem iron cleaves the drug's endoperoxide bridge, generating reactive carbon radicals that alkylate parasite proteins and lipids, producing a rapid blood-stage kill.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are artemisinins always given as combination therapy (ACT) rather than alone?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They have a very short duration of action, so they are paired with a long-acting partner drug (e.g. lumefantrine) that clears residual parasites and helps protect against resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is first-line treatment for UNCOMPLICATED falciparum malaria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Oral artemisinin combination therapy (ACT) - e.g. artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet), taken over 3 days.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet) be taken with fat or food?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Lumefantrine absorption is fat-dependent, so taking it with food/fatty meals ensures adequate drug levels.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is first-line treatment for SEVERE / complicated falciparum malaria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: IV artesunate - it has replaced IV quinine. Oral ACT is then given to complete the course.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drug is used for severe malaria in a pregnant woman, and in which trimesters?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: IV artesunate is recommended for severe malaria in ALL trimesters of pregnancy. (Oral Riamet is generally avoided in the first trimester unless there is no alternative.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: After treating severe malaria with IV artesunate, what blood test must be monitored and for how long?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: FBC - check weekly for about 4 weeks, to detect post-artesunate DELAYED HAEMOLYSIS.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which component of Riamet can prolong the QT interval, and what should you avoid co-prescribing?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Lumefantrine prolongs the QT interval. Avoid other QT-prolonging drugs and halofantrine (fatal QT risk).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) work as malaria prophylaxis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Atovaquone collapses the parasite's mitochondrial membrane potential (potentiated by proguanil). It kills both liver and blood stages (causal prophylaxis), which is why it has a short tail after travel.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the main selling point of Malarone as malaria prophylaxis regarding its 'tail'?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A short tail - start 1-2 days before travel and continue only 7 days after returning, versus 4 weeks for doxycycline and mefloquine. It is also well tolerated and convenient.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How should Malarone be taken, and in whom is it avoided?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Take once daily with food or a milky drink (absorption is fat-dependent). Avoid in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) for prophylaxis, and in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which cheap tetracycline is used for malaria prophylaxis, and how long is it continued after travel?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Doxycycline 100 mg once daily. Start 1-2 days before travel and continue for 4 WEEKS after leaving the malarial area.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A traveller on doxycycline prophylaxis to a sunny country develops a rash on sun-exposed skin. What is the cause and advice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Photosensitivity - a well-known doxycycline side effect. Advise sun protection (cover up, high-factor sunscreen). Also take it upright with water to avoid oesophagitis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In whom is doxycycline malaria prophylaxis contraindicated?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Pregnancy and children under 12 (it affects developing teeth and bone).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should doxycycline be separated from antacids, iron tablets, and dairy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Divalent/cation-containing products (calcium, iron, antacids, milk) chelate doxycycline and reduce its absorption, so doses must be separated.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which antimalarial is taken WEEKLY for prophylaxis in chloroquine-resistant areas?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Mefloquine - once weekly. Start 2-3 weeks before travel (to assess tolerability) and continue 4 weeks after return.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which antimalarial is the prophylaxis of CHOICE in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Mefloquine (all trimesters), used when doxycycline and Malarone are avoided in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What class of side effects is mefloquine famous for, and how can they present?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Neuropsychiatric effects - vivid/abnormal dreams, anxiety, depression, psychosis, suicidal ideation and seizures. They can persist for months to years or be permanent after stopping.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In which patients should mefloquine be avoided?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Anyone with a history of psychiatric illness (depression, anxiety, psychosis) or epilepsy/seizures. It is also contraindicated with halofantrine (fatal QT).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Compare the post-travel 'tails' of the three main malaria prophylaxis options.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Malarone (atovaquone-proguanil): continue only 7 days after return. Doxycycline and mefloquine: continue 4 weeks after return. The short Malarone tail is its key advantage.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is mefloquine started 2-3 weeks before travel rather than just before?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: To assess tolerability - so that if the traveller develops neuropsychiatric side effects, there is time to switch to an alternative before departure. Patients are given an alert card.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which antimalarial is the only agent that clears the dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale, and what is this called?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Primaquine (an 8-aminoquinoline). It kills the dormant liver hypnozoites -> 'radical cure' / relapse prevention. No other standard antimalarial can do this.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient has completed treatment for P. vivax malaria. Why is primaquine added, and when is it given?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: To eradicate the dormant liver hypnozoites and prevent relapse ('radical cure'). It is given AFTER blood-stage treatment is complete (it does not treat the acute blood-stage illness). Typical regimen ~30 mg base once daily for 14 days.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides radical cure, what additional useful antimalarial effect does primaquine have?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is gametocytocidal -> a single low dose is transmission-blocking (kills the sexual forms) in falciparum malaria, reducing spread to mosquitoes.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What test MUST you check before prescribing primaquine, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Quantify G6PD activity first. In G6PD deficiency, primaquine causes severe haemolysis. Intermediate deficiency may allow a modified weekly regimen under specialist advice.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is primaquine avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The fetal/infant G6PD status is unknown, so there is a risk of causing severe haemolysis in the baby. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Apart from haemolysis, name another important toxicity of primaquine.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Methaemoglobinaemia (plus GI upset). The dominant safety concern remains haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
