pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What single-dose alternative to primaquine can be used for radical cure of vivax malaria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Tafenoquine (also an 8-aminoquinoline) offers single-dose radical cure. Like primaquine it needs G6PD checked first because of haemolysis risk in deficiency.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does ivermectin kill parasites, and why are mammals spared?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It opens invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels -> paralyses and kills the parasite. Mammals lack these channels and also keep the drug out of the CNS at the blood-brain barrier, giving selectivity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the main indications for oral ivermectin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Strongyloides, onchocerciasis (river blindness), other nematodes, scabies (especially crusted/Norwegian scabies or when topical treatment fails) and head lice.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When is ivermectin preferred for scabies rather than topical treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: In crusted (Norwegian) scabies, or when topical treatment fails or is impractical. Usually a single weight-based oral dose, often repeated at 1-2 weeks.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Before treating onchocerciasis with ivermectin, which co-infection must you screen for, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Loa loa. A high Loa loa microfilarial load plus ivermectin can trigger a fatal encephalopathy, so screen for it first.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient treated for onchocerciasis with ivermectin develops itching and rash. What is this?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A Mazzotti reaction - itch/rash from dying microfilariae. It is expected in onchocerciasis and reflects the parasites being killed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do benzimidazoles (mebendazole/albendazole) kill worms?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind parasite beta-tubulin -> block microtubule formation and glucose uptake -> the worm is starved and immobilised and dies.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line drug for threadworm (Enterobius), and how is it dosed?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Mebendazole - a single 100 mg dose, REPEATED in 2 weeks. Treat the whole household simultaneously and add hygiene measures (handwashing, laundering, keeping nails short).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides threadworm, which intestinal worm infections does mebendazole treat?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Roundworm (Ascaris), hookworm and whipworm - the common intestinal nematodes.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which benzimidazole is used for tissue (systemic) worm disease, and for what?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Albendazole - used for hydatid disease (Echinococcus) and neurocysticercosis, given as longer courses rather than a single dose.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What must accompany albendazole treatment of neurocysticercosis, and what must be excluded first?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Give concurrent corticosteroids (dexamethasone) - killing the cysts provokes inflammation - and add anticonvulsants if needed. Exclude ocular cysts before treating.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are mebendazole and albendazole avoided in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are teratogenic, especially albendazole and especially in the first trimester. Use effective contraception during and for about a month after albendazole.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What monitoring is needed for prolonged albendazole courses?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Check FBC and LFTs before and during treatment - long courses can cause raised LFTs and bone-marrow suppression.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does praziquantel kill worms?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It increases parasite membrane calcium permeability -> tetanic contraction/spastic paralysis plus tegument damage -> the worm dies.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the drug of choice for schistosomiasis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Praziquantel, given as a weight-based oral dose (single or split over a day). It also treats tapeworm (cestode) infections such as Taenia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why might praziquantel need to be repeated in acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Praziquantel only kills ADULT worms and is ineffective against immature/migrating schistosomes. A repeat dose is given once those worms have matured.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What key caution applies to praziquantel in ocular cysticercosis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Destroying the parasite in the eye can cause irreversible eye damage. In neurocysticercosis give with corticosteroids under specialist care.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drug interaction effectively contraindicates co-prescribing with praziquantel?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Rifampicin markedly lowers praziquantel levels -> avoid the combination (treatment failure). Other enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, dexamethasone) also reduce levels.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drug is the key antiprotozoal for Giardia, amoebiasis and Trichomonas?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Metronidazole (full profile covered elsewhere). Remember: no alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction); for amoebiasis follow with a luminal amoebicide to clear cysts.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They irreversibly block the H+/K+-ATPase ('proton pump') on gastric parietal cells — the final common step of acid secretion. This gives profound, long-lasting acid suppression: the most effective acid-reducing drugs available.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why should a PPI be taken 30-60 minutes BEFORE food?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: PPIs only inhibit proton pumps that are actively secreting acid. A meal recruits pumps into action, so taking the PPI shortly before eating means the maximum number of active pumps are exposed to the drug and inhibited.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A PPI has a short plasma half-life (~1-2 h), yet is dosed once daily. Why does its effect last over 24 hours?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Because it binds the proton pump irreversibly (covalently). Acid suppression persists long after the drug has cleared the plasma — recovery requires synthesis of new pumps, so a single daily dose gives 24 h+ acid control.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: List the main indications for a PPI.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: GORD/reflux oesophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, part of H. pylori eradication, NSAID gastroprotection (at-risk patients only), uninvestigated dyspepsia, high-dose IV after endoscopy for a bleeding ulcer, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is a PPI used to treat GORD / reflux oesophagitis over time?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Give a full dose for 4-8 weeks to heal the oesophagus, then step down to the lowest effective dose or switch to on-demand use. Review the ongoing need rather than continuing full-dose indefinitely.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which patients on an NSAID should be co-prescribed a PPI for gastroprotection?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: At-risk patients only: age >65, previous peptic ulcer or GI bleed, high-dose NSAID, or on concurrent steroids or an anticoagulant. Routine gastroprotection is not needed for every NSAID user.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient has an actively bleeding peptic ulcer. How is a PPI used, and at what point?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: High-dose IV PPI (e.g. omeprazole 80 mg then an 8 mg/h infusion) given AFTER endoscopic treatment of the bleeding ulcer — not routinely before endoscopy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A 58-year-old presents with new dyspepsia, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. Why is simply starting an empirical PPI unsafe?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: PPIs can mask the symptoms of gastric cancer. Alarm/ALARM features (anaemia, weight loss, anorexia, recent-onset progressive symptoms, melaena/haematemesis, dysphagia, or age >55) warrant urgent 2-week-wait endoscopy BEFORE starting an empirical PPI.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the 'alarm features' in dyspepsia that mandate urgent endoscopy rather than empirical PPI therapy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Anaemia, unintentional weight loss, anorexia, recent-onset progressive symptoms, melaena/haematemesis (GI bleeding), and dysphagia — plus age >55. Any of these needs urgent 2-week-wait endoscopy to exclude cancer.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are typical oral maintenance doses of omeprazole and lansoprazole you should recognise?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Omeprazole 20-40 mg once daily; lansoprazole 15-30 mg once daily. (Contrast with high-dose IV — e.g. omeprazole 80 mg then infusion — used after endoscopy for a bleeding ulcer.)

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which electrolyte disturbance is subject to an MHRA warning with long-term PPI use, and how does it present?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hypomagnesaemia (low Mg2+), especially after >1 year or with digoxin/diuretics. It causes muscle cramps and can precipitate arrhythmias. Check magnesium in patients on long-term PPIs, particularly those on digoxin or diuretics.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Beyond magnesium, what long-term deficiencies and infection risks are associated with PPIs?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Reduced calcium absorption (increased fracture/osteoporosis risk), B12 and iron deficiency, hyponatraemia, and increased risk of C. difficile and other GI infections (from loss of the acid barrier).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient stops a long-term PPI abruptly and their reflux symptoms flare worse than before. What has happened?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Rebound acid hypersecretion — stopping the PPI triggers a transient surge in acid production. This is why long courses are best stepped down or tapered rather than stopped suddenly, and it can be mistaken for ongoing disease.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Name two rare but exam-relevant adverse effects of PPIs (one renal, one dermatological).
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Acute interstitial nephritis (rare renal cause of a rising creatinine) and subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (an MHRA-flagged photosensitive rash).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on clopidogrel after a stent needs gastroprotection. Which PPI should you AVOID and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole — they reduce clopidogrel's activation, weakening its antiplatelet effect and risking stent thrombosis. Prefer lansoprazole or pantoprazole instead.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does raising gastric pH with a PPI affect the absorption of certain other drugs?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Some drugs need an acidic stomach to be absorbed, so a PPI reduces their absorption and efficacy — e.g. itraconazole/ketoconazole and certain HIV drugs (atazanavir, rilpivirine). Rilpivirine is contraindicated with PPIs.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which drug levels can a PPI RAISE, and which effect can compound one of them?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: PPIs can raise digoxin and methotrexate levels. The digoxin rise is compounded by PPI-induced hypomagnesaemia (low Mg2+ increases digoxin toxicity risk) — another reason to check magnesium.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What monitoring is appropriate for a patient on long-term PPI therapy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Check magnesium (especially with digoxin or diuretics) and B12/iron. Crucially, regularly REVIEW the ongoing need and deprescribe long courses — PPIs are frequently continued without indication.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: An elderly patient has been on omeprazole for 3 years with no clear current indication. What is the appropriate action?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Review and deprescribe. Step down or stop (tapering to limit rebound acid), reserving continued PPI use for a genuine indication — this reduces long-term risks such as low Mg2+/B12, fractures and C. difficile.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the mechanism of action of H2 receptor antagonists such as famotidine and cimetidine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They competitively block histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing acid secretion (mainly basal and nocturnal). This makes them less potent acid suppressors than PPIs.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Are H2 receptor antagonists more or less potent at suppressing gastric acid than PPIs?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Less potent. H2 antagonists reduce mainly basal/nocturnal acid, so they are used second-line or as an adjunct when a PPI is not tolerated or not wanted.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why do H2 receptor antagonists lose effectiveness with continuous daily use, and how does this affect dosing?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Tolerance (tachyphylaxis) develops within days to weeks of continuous use. This is why they suit intermittent or nocturnal (as-required) dosing rather than long-term regular use.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Where do H2 receptor antagonists sit in the management of GORD, dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are a second-line option or adjunct, used when a PPI is not tolerated or not wanted. They can also be added at night to a PPI to control nocturnal acid breakthrough.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is ranitidine no longer used, and what has replaced it?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Ranitidine was withdrawn because of contamination with the probable carcinogen NDMA. Famotidine is now the usual H2 antagonist of choice.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on a daytime PPI still wakes with acid symptoms overnight. What can be added?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A night-time H2 receptor antagonist (e.g. famotidine) can be added to control nocturnal acid breakthrough that the PPI alone is not covering.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the common side effects of famotidine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is generally well tolerated. Recognised side effects include headache, GI upset (e.g. diarrhoea or constipation) and dizziness.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does famotidine need dose adjustment in renal impairment, and what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Famotidine is renally cleared, so it can accumulate if renal function is poor. Check renal function and reduce the dose in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is a typical dose of famotidine for acid-related symptoms?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Around 20-40 mg once or twice daily, often taken at night. The dose should be reduced in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which H2 receptor antagonist causes gynaecomastia and anti-androgen effects, and why does this matter?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cimetidine. It has anti-androgen effects causing gynaecomastia (and sometimes sexual dysfunction), which is one reason famotidine is now preferred.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is cimetidine avoided in patients taking warfarin, phenytoin or theophylline?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cimetidine inhibits the metabolism of other drugs, raising warfarin, phenytoin and theophylline levels and risking toxicity (e.g. bleeding, phenytoin/theophylline toxicity). Famotidine does not do this, so it is preferred.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: An elderly patient with renal impairment on cimetidine becomes confused. What is the likely cause?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cimetidine can cause confusion or delirium, particularly in the elderly and in renal impairment. Stopping it (and switching to famotidine) is the appropriate action.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do H2 receptor antagonists compare with PPIs, and why is famotidine preferred over cimetidine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: H2 antagonists give weaker acid suppression than PPIs and lose effect through tolerance, so they are second-line/adjunct. Famotidine is preferred over cimetidine because cimetidine causes gynaecomastia, inhibits metabolism of other drugs (raising warfarin/phenytoin/theophylline levels) and can cause confusion in the elderly.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the first-line regimen for H. pylori eradication in a patient with a peptic ulcer, and how long is it given?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 7-day triple therapy: a PPI twice daily + amoxicillin 1 g BD + clarithromycin 500 mg BD. The course lasts 7 days.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does H. pylori eradication combine a PPI with two antibiotics rather than using an antibiotic alone?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: The PPI reduces acid so the antibiotics can work and the mucosa can heal. Two antibiotics are used to eradicate the organism and to prevent development of resistance.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In the first-line triple regimen, what is the role of the PPI specifically?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It suppresses gastric acid, which allows the antibiotics to work effectively and lets the ulcer/mucosa heal. It is given twice daily alongside the two antibiotics.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient needing H. pylori eradication reports a penicillin allergy. How do you modify the standard triple therapy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Swap amoxicillin for metronidazole. The regimen becomes a PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole (metronidazole 400 mg BD) for 7 days.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient needing H. pylori eradication had a course of clarithromycin (a macrolide) last year. Why does this change your choice, and what do you use?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Previous macrolide exposure means likely clarithromycin resistance, so avoid any clarithromycin-based regimen. Use a PPI + amoxicillin + metronidazole, or bismuth quadruple therapy instead.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: List the main indications for H. pylori eradication therapy.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori-positive dyspepsia, MALT lymphoma, and after an H. pylori-associated bleeding ulcer.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which test is used to confirm successful H. pylori eradication, and which test should NOT be used for this?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Use a urea breath test (or stool antigen test). Do NOT use serology to confirm eradication, as antibodies persist after the organism is cleared.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: You are arranging a urea breath test to confirm H. pylori eradication. What timing rules avoid a false negative?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Perform it at least 4 weeks after finishing the antibiotics AND at least 2 weeks after stopping the PPI. Recent antibiotics or PPI suppress the organism and give false negatives.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: After which clinical scenarios should eradication be confirmed with a breath/stool test?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: After a bleeding ulcer, in MALT lymphoma, and where symptoms persist despite treatment.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on long-term simvastatin is about to start clarithromycin-based triple therapy. What must you do?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Clarithromycin inhibits the metabolism of simvastatin, raising levels and the risk of rhabdomyolysis. Simvastatin is contraindicated with clarithromycin, so withhold the statin during the course.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Beyond statins, which two commonly monitored drugs are affected by clarithromycin's inhibition of drug metabolism, and how?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It raises warfarin levels (INR goes up, bleeding risk) and raises digoxin levels. Monitor INR closely and watch for digoxin toxicity.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What cardiac caution applies to clarithromycin in H. pylori eradication?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Clarithromycin prolongs the QT interval. Use with caution in cardiac disease and in patients already on other QT-prolonging drugs, as this risks arrhythmia.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on metronidazole-containing eradication therapy asks whether they can drink alcohol. What do you advise and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Avoid alcohol during the course and for 48 hours after. Metronidazole with alcohol causes a disulfiram reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the common side effects a patient should expect on triple therapy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Diarrhoea and GI upset, taste disturbance (clarithromycin/metronidazole). Watch for C. difficile diarrhoea and candidiasis (thrush).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: First-line H. pylori therapy has failed. What is the second-line regimen and how long is it given?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Bismuth quadruple therapy: a PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline for 10-14 days. Use antibiotics not used in the first-line course.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Besides first-line failure, when else is bismuth quadruple therapy chosen for H. pylori?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: When there is penicillin allergy or previous macrolide (clarithromycin) exposure, since it avoids both amoxicillin and clarithromycin.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on bismuth quadruple therapy is alarmed by black stools and a darkened tongue. What do you tell them?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: This is a harmless, expected effect of bismuth that resolves after treatment. Reassure them it is not bleeding or a dangerous sign.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What key contraindications and cautions apply to the tetracycline in quadruple therapy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Tetracycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 12, and causes photosensitivity. Its absorption is reduced by chelation with the co-given bismuth, antacids, iron, calcium and dairy, so separate the doses.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do 5-HT3 antagonists (e.g. ondansetron) work as antiemetics?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They block 5-HT3 (serotonin) receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) and on vagal afferents in the gut. This blocks the serotonin released from enterochromaffin cells by chemotherapy, radiation or surgery -> potent antiemetic effect.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the two main first-line indications for ondansetron?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Chemotherapy/radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) and post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV). It is first-line for both.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, what is ondansetron usually combined with?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Dexamethasone. For highly emetogenic chemotherapy add an NK1 antagonist (+/- olanzapine).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is ondansetron a poor choice for motion sickness or vestibular nausea?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 5-HT3 antagonists work at the CTZ and gut, not the vestibular pathway, so they are less useful for motion sickness and other vestibular/labyrinthine causes.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the very common bowel side effect of ondansetron, and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Constipation, because blocking 5-HT3 receptors slows gut motility. Headache and flushing are also common.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What cardiac adverse effect must you watch for with ondansetron, and when should you avoid it?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: QT prolongation. Avoid in congenital long-QT syndrome, with other QT-prolonging drugs, or with electrolyte disturbance; check ECG/electrolytes if there is cardiac risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is ondansetron used with caution in the first trimester of pregnancy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: There is a small signal for cleft palate, so it is best avoided in early pregnancy where possible.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on an SSRI is prescribed ondansetron and tramadol. What serious reaction is the concern?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Serotonin syndrome. 5-HT3 antagonists add to the serotonergic load of SSRIs/SNRIs and tramadol.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is a typical ondansetron dose for PONV versus regular use, and the max single IV dose?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A common single PONV dose is 4 mg IV; regular dosing is 4-8 mg PO/IV (e.g. 8 mg BD). Max single IV dose is 16 mg, diluted and given over at least 15 minutes.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which 5-HT3 antagonist is long-acting and used for delayed CINV?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Palonosetron - it is long-acting with high receptor affinity, making it useful for delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does metoclopramide work as an antiemetic?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a central D2 (dopamine) antagonist at the CTZ, plus it has a prokinetic effect that speeds gastric emptying. At high doses it also has some 5-HT3 antagonist action.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: For which types of nausea is metoclopramide especially useful?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Nausea with gastric stasis, migraine (it also aids absorption of analgesics), and opioid-induced or GI causes. It is not used for motion sickness.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does metoclopramide cause extrapyramidal side effects when domperidone does not?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Metoclopramide crosses the blood-brain barrier and blocks central dopamine receptors, so it can cause acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia. Domperidone does not cross the BBB, so it causes minimal EPS.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A young woman given metoclopramide develops a sustained upward gaze and neck spasm. What is this?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Acute dystonia (e.g. oculogyric crisis), an extrapyramidal reaction. It is more common in young women, children and young adults.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why should metoclopramide be avoided in Parkinson's disease?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Its central dopamine blockade worsens the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. Use domperidone instead if an antiemetic/prokinetic is needed.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What endocrine side effect can metoclopramide cause?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hyperprolactinaemia, which can present as galactorrhoea, due to central dopamine blockade.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the MHRA duration and age restrictions on metoclopramide?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Short-term use only (up to 5 days) to limit extrapyramidal and neurological risk, and it is restricted in under-18s. Usual dose is 10 mg up to TDS, max 30 mg/day.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why should metoclopramide be avoided in bowel obstruction?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Its prokinetic action stimulates gut motility, which is dangerous in bowel obstruction or perforation (also avoid after recent GI surgery/haemorrhage).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does domperidone differ from metoclopramide in terms of the blood-brain barrier?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Domperidone is a peripheral D2 antagonist that does NOT cross the blood-brain barrier, so it has minimal extrapyramidal effects. Metoclopramide does cross the BBB and causes EPS.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is domperidone the antiemetic of choice in Parkinson's disease?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It blocks dopamine at the CTZ but does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it controls nausea without worsening Parkinson's motor symptoms. It is also useful to counter dopamine-agonist-induced nausea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the key safety concern that limits domperidone use?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: QT prolongation with risk of serious ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death (MHRA warning). Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest course (max ~1 week).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In whom should domperidone be avoided because of its cardiac risk?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Patients with existing cardiac disease/QT prolongation, significant hepatic impairment, or those taking other QT-prolonging drugs or drugs that strongly inhibit its metabolism.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is a typical domperidone dose and course length?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 10 mg TDS, max 30 mg/day, for up to about 1 week, at the lowest effective dose because of the cardiac risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do phenothiazines like prochlorperazine work as antiemetics?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are central D2 (dopamine) antagonists at the CTZ with additional antihistamine and antimuscarinic actions, giving a broad antiemetic effect.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which type of nausea are phenothiazines like prochlorperazine particularly useful for?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Vestibular/labyrinthine nausea - vertigo, Meniere's disease and motion sickness - as well as general nausea and vomiting.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is a practical advantage of prochlorperazine's buccal (Buccastem) formulation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It can be absorbed through the buccal mucosa, useful when a patient is vomiting and cannot keep oral tablets down (e.g. 3-6 mg buccal BD). IM is used for acute severe nausea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What side-effect profile do phenothiazine antiemetics share with antipsychotics?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Extrapyramidal effects, sedation, postural hypotension (alpha blockade), QT prolongation, hyperprolactinaemia and photosensitivity; rarely neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In which two patient groups should phenothiazines like prochlorperazine be avoided?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Parkinson's disease (dopamine blockade worsens it) and elderly patients with dementia (increased risk of stroke and death, as with all antipsychotics).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does cyclizine work as an antiemetic, and what receptors does it act on?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is an antihistamine (H1 antagonist) with antimuscarinic action. It blocks signals from the vestibular system and the vomiting centre, making it effective in motion/vestibular and mechanical causes of nausea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is cyclizine considered a good broad 'first-line' ward antiemetic? Name several situations it covers.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It works across a wide range of causes: motion sickness, vertigo/labyrinthine disorders, raised intracranial pressure, mechanical bowel obstruction, and postoperative nausea/vomiting (PONV). This broad coverage makes it a sensible general first-line choice.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient with heart failure and a recent MI needs an antiemetic. Why be cautious with cyclizine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cyclizine can cause tachycardia (reducing cardiac output) and, given rapidly IV, palpitations. It can also counteract the beneficial haemodynamic effects of opioids. Use caution in severe heart failure and recent MI.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the main side effects of cyclizine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Sedation, antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation), and tachycardia (especially with rapid IV -> palpitations). It can be euphoriant, which is one reason it may be misused.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which pre-existing conditions make you cautious about the antimuscarinic effects of cyclizine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Prostatic enlargement (risk of urinary retention) and angle-closure glaucoma. These are classic antimuscarinic cautions.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is a typical dose and route for cyclizine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 50 mg three times a day (TDS), given PO, IM, or IV. Give IV doses slowly, as rapid injection can cause palpitations.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does promethazine work as an antiemetic?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a sedating H1 antihistamine (with antimuscarinic and anti-D2 activity) that acts on the vomiting centre and vestibular pathways.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: For nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, what is the first-line drug class, and what are the options?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: An antihistamine (cyclizine or promethazine) or prochlorperazine is first-line. Metoclopramide or ondansetron are second-line for short-term use.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In hyperemesis gravidarum, what two supportive measures should be added alongside an antiemetic?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Thiamine (to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy) and VTE prophylaxis (pregnancy plus dehydration raises clot risk).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is promethazine contraindicated in children under 2 years old?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It can cause fatal respiratory depression in this age group.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the main practical downside of promethazine, and what else is it used for?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Marked sedation/drowsiness (plus antimuscarinic effects and dizziness). Besides motion sickness, vertigo and nausea of pregnancy, it is also used for sedation and allergy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is dexamethasone used in the management of nausea and vomiting?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: As an adjunct that boosts other antiemetics. It is used in chemotherapy-induced nausea (with a 5-HT3 antagonist, sometimes plus an NK1 antagonist), for PONV prophylaxis, and for nausea from raised intracranial pressure (by reducing cerebral oedema).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is dexamethasone particularly useful for nausea caused by raised intracranial pressure?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: As a corticosteroid it reduces cerebral oedema, relieving the underlying cause of the nausea (given with a PPI at higher doses).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the key side effect to watch for when using dexamethasone as an antiemetic, and who is most at risk?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hyperglycaemia. Monitor blood glucose, especially in diabetics, particularly with repeated dosing. Single doses are generally well tolerated.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient reports perineal/perianal tingling during a rapid IV dexamethasone dose for PONV. Is this dangerous?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No, it is a harmless, transient effect of rapid IV administration. Other single-dose effects include insomnia and mood change; more serious steroid effects appear with repeated dosing.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do NK1 antagonists (aprepitant, fosaprepitant) work, and what type of chemotherapy nausea are they especially good for?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are NK1 (neurokinin-1 / substance P) receptor antagonists, blocking substance P in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vomiting centre. They are especially effective against delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In highly emetogenic chemotherapy, what 'triple therapy' regimen prevents nausea and vomiting?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: An NK1 antagonist (aprepitant/fosaprepitant) added to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone. This covers both acute and delayed nausea/vomiting.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why must women on an NK1 antagonist (aprepitant) use additional contraception?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Aprepitant alters drug metabolism and reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraception, so an additional (non-hormonal) method is needed during and for a period after treatment.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: An NK1 antagonist is co-prescribed with dexamethasone for chemotherapy. What dosing adjustment is needed and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Aprepitant raises dexamethasone levels, so the dexamethasone dose should be halved to avoid excessive steroid exposure.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do NK1 antagonists affect warfarin and phenytoin?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They reduce the effect of warfarin and phenytoin. Monitor the INR (e.g. around 2 weeks after the chemo cycle) as anticoagulation may be reduced.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the difference between hyoscine butylbromide and hyoscine hydrobromide in terms of getting into the brain?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Butylbromide (Buscopan) is a charged (quaternary) molecule that poorly enters the CNS -> acts peripherally. Hydrobromide is lipophilic (tertiary amine) and crosses the blood-brain barrier -> acts centrally, e.g. as an antiemetic for motion sickness.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the main uses of hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: As a peripheral antispasmodic for GI, biliary and renal colic and IBS smooth-muscle spasm, and to reduce secretions/'death rattle' in palliative care.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which hyoscine salt is used for motion sickness, and in what form?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hyoscine hydrobromide, as a transdermal patch. It crosses the blood-brain barrier to act centrally; it is also used to reduce secretions in palliative care.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the antimuscarinic contraindications common to the hyoscines?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Angle-closure glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, prostatic enlargement/urinary retention, and paralytic ileus or GI obstruction.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What MHRA safety warning applies to hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) injection?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: The injection can cause serious cardiac adverse events (e.g. from tachycardia); avoid it in patients with tachycardia or underlying cardiac disease. Monitor those at risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What antimuscarinic side effects can the hyoscines cause, and who is especially prone to confusion?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention and constipation. Confusion is a particular risk in the elderly, especially with hydrobromide (which crosses the blood-brain barrier).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Name the five main classes of oral/rectal laxatives and give one example of each.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Bulk-forming (ispaghula/Fybogel), osmotic (macrogol, lactulose), stimulant (senna, bisacodyl), stool softener (docusate), and rectal preparations (glycerol suppositories, phosphate enemas).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What single clinical situation means ALL laxatives should be avoided?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Suspected intestinal obstruction. All laxative classes are contraindicated if obstruction is suspected.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl) work?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They stimulate the colonic myenteric plexus and promote fluid/electrolyte secretion into the bowel, increasing peristalsis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: When should a stimulant laxative such as senna be taken, and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: At night. Onset is 6-12 hours, so a nocte dose produces a morning bowel motion.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on long-term high-dose senna develops muscle weakness and an arrhythmia. What electrolyte problem should you suspect?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hypokalaemia. Chronic stimulant laxative overuse causes potassium loss, which can worsen and present with weakness and arrhythmia.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the most common troublesome side effect of stimulant laxatives?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cramping/abdominal pain (with diarrhoea); overuse can cause hypokalaemia.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is stimulant-induced hypokalaemia dangerous in a patient taking digoxin?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Low K+ potentiates digoxin toxicity. It also adds to K+ loss from loop/thiazide diuretics and corticosteroids.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which laxative combination is used first-line for opioid-induced constipation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: An osmotic laxative plus a stimulant. Bulk-forming laxatives are avoided in opioid-induced constipation.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does lactulose relieve constipation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a non-absorbed osmotic disaccharide that draws water into the bowel; it is also fermented by colonic bacteria.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Besides constipation, what important condition does lactulose treat, and by what mechanism?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hepatic encephalopathy. Colonic fermentation acidifies the lumen, trapping ammonia as ammonium (NH4+) so gut-derived ammonia is excreted rather than absorbed.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the dosing endpoint when using lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Titrate the dose to achieve 2-3 soft stools per day.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is lactulose generally avoided in irritable bowel syndrome?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Colonic fermentation causes bloating and flatulence, which worsens IBS symptoms.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the main downsides of lactulose as a laxative?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Bloating, flatulence and cramps from fermentation, plus a slow onset of around 48 hours; overuse can cause dehydration/electrolyte disturbance.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does macrogol (Movicol/Laxido) work as a laxative?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is polyethylene glycol (PEG) that binds water and carries it through the bowel, softening stool and increasing volume; it is supplied with balancing electrolytes so there is no net fluid/electrolyte loss.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which osmotic laxative is first-line for chronic constipation, and why is it well tolerated?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Macrogol. It is electrolyte-balanced, so it is generally well tolerated (bloating/nausea are the main effects); ensure adequate fluid intake.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What high-dose regimen is macrogol used for in a patient with faecal impaction?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A 'disimpaction' regimen using escalating high doses (up to about 8 sachets/day) to clear the impacted stool.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does ispaghula (Fybogel) relieve constipation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a bulk-forming soluble fibre that absorbs water to increase faecal mass, stimulating peristalsis; onset is over days.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What key administration instruction must accompany a bulk-forming laxative like ispaghula?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Take with plenty of fluid (a full glass of water) and not immediately before bed, to avoid oesophageal or bowel obstruction.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In which patients is ispaghula a good choice for constipation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Constipation with a low-fibre diet that cannot be improved by diet, and to regulate stool in IBS, diverticular disease or a stoma.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why should ispaghula be avoided in intestinal obstruction, faecal impaction or reduced gut motility?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: The added bulk cannot pass and risks worsening obstruction, especially if taken without enough fluid.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is a bulk-forming laxative the wrong choice for opioid-induced constipation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Opioids reduce gut motility, so added bulk can worsen constipation/obstruction; use an osmotic plus a stimulant instead.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the main advantage of rectal laxatives (glycerol suppositories, phosphate enemas) over oral agents?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Rapid relief of a loaded rectum, with onset in minutes to about 1 hour.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do glycerol suppositories and phosphate enemas act?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Glycerol suppositories are mildly irritant and osmotic; phosphate enemas draw water into the rectum osmotically, producing rapid rectal evacuation.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What dangerous adverse effects can phosphate enemas cause, and in whom?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Fluid/electrolyte shifts (hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia) and acute kidney injury, which the MHRA warns can be fatal, especially in the elderly, renal impairment, dehydration or colitis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which co-prescribed drugs increase the risk of AKI/electrolyte disturbance with a phosphate enema, and what should you check?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics and NSAIDs. Check U&Es and use with care in at-risk patients.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which rectal preparation must be avoided in a patient with peanut or soya allergy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Arachis (peanut) oil enema.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does docusate work, and when is it particularly useful?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a stool softener/surfactant (with mild stimulant action) that lets water and fat penetrate stool, softening it; useful where straining must be avoided, e.g. post-MI, haemorrhoids, post-surgery.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is docusate often combined with a stimulant laxative?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: As a sole agent it is mild with weak efficacy, so it is frequently paired with a stimulant for adequate effect.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does linaclotide relieve constipation, and what is its main use?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It increases intestinal fluid secretion (and dampens visceral pain), making it useful for IBS with constipation (IBS-C) when other laxatives have failed.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is linaclotide taken and what is its commonest side effect?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 290 micrograms once daily at least 30 minutes before food; it commonly causes diarrhoea, which should prompt stopping and review if severe/prolonged (dehydration risk).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does prucalopride work, and what makes it safer than older prokinetics?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a selective 5-HT4 agonist prokinetic that stimulates colonic motility; being selective, it avoids the cardiac risk associated with older prokinetics such as cisapride.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: When is prucalopride indicated for chronic constipation?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: When at least 2 laxatives from different classes, each tried for at least 6 months, have failed. Common side effects are headache, nausea and diarrhoea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What type of drug is loperamide and how does it work?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A peripheral opioid (mu) receptor agonist acting on the myenteric plexus of the gut. It slows peristalsis, giving more time for water absorption, so stools become firmer and less frequent.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does loperamide not cause sedation, analgesia or dependence at normal doses?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It does not cross the blood-brain barrier (it is actively effluxed there), so it acts only on gut opioid receptors with no central effect. This is why it is a purely antidiarrhoeal opioid rather than an analgesic.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: For what kind of diarrhoea is loperamide used?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Symptomatic relief of acute or chronic non-infective diarrhoea - e.g. IBS-D, high ileostomy output, and chemotherapy-related diarrhoea. It is first-line for troublesome diarrhoea where infection or inflammation is not the cause.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In which types of diarrhoea must loperamide be AVOIDED, and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Avoid in acute inflammatory colitis, severe ulcerative colitis, C. difficile, and bloody or feverish diarrhoea. Slowing the gut in these settings risks toxic megacolon and prolongs the infection.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient with bloody, feverish diarrhoea asks for loperamide to stop the frequency. Is this appropriate?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No. Bloody/feverish diarrhoea suggests an infective or inflammatory cause, where loperamide risks toxic megacolon and prolongs infection. Treat the underlying cause rather than slowing the gut.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is loperamide dosed for diarrhoea (prescribed)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool, up to a maximum of 16 mg/day (over-the-counter limits are lower).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the common side effects of loperamide at normal doses?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Constipation, bloating and abdominal cramps - all extensions of its gut-slowing effect.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What serious harm can occur with high-dose loperamide misuse or overdose?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: QT prolongation and QRS widening leading to dangerous arrhythmias (torsades, Brugada-pattern) and even cardiac arrest. This is the basis of the MHRA warning against high-dose loperamide misuse.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why might a drug that inhibits loperamide's efflux at the blood-brain barrier increase its toxicity?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Such drugs overwhelm the transporter that normally keeps loperamide out of the brain and lowers its plasma levels, raising CNS and cardiac exposure. This increases the risk of central effects and cardiotoxicity, including QT prolongation.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does codeine slow diarrhoea, and how does this differ from loperamide?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Codeine is an opioid that stimulates gut opioid receptors to slow motility, but unlike loperamide it crosses the blood-brain barrier. This gives it central effects - sedation, dependence and respiratory depression.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is loperamide usually preferred over codeine as an antidiarrhoeal?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Both slow the gut, but codeine crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes sedation, dependence and respiratory depression, whereas loperamide does not. Loperamide gives the antidiarrhoeal effect without central opioid harms.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Codeine is a prodrug - what does this mean for its effect between different patients?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Codeine is converted in the body to morphine, its active form, but the amount varies between people. Some convert very little and get little effect, while some convert a lot and can develop morphine toxicity.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Can codeine be used as an antidiarrhoeal in a child under 12, or in infective colitis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No. Codeine is contraindicated in children under 12. Like loperamide, it must not be used in infective or inflammatory diarrhoea, where slowing the gut is harmful.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does colestyramine work as an antidiarrhoeal?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a bile-acid sequestrant that binds bile acids in the gut lumen so they are excreted rather than reabsorbed. This stops bile acids irritating the colon in bile-acid malabsorption.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which patients benefit from colestyramine for diarrhoea?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Those with bile-acid malabsorption diarrhoea - after terminal ileal disease or resection (e.g. Crohn's), post-cholecystectomy, or bile-acid diarrhoea. It is also used for cholestatic pruritus (itch).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient with Crohn's who had a terminal ileal resection now has watery diarrhoea. What antidiarrhoeal targets the likely mechanism?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Colestyramine. Terminal ileal loss causes bile-acid malabsorption, and colestyramine binds the excess bile acids that would otherwise irritate the colon and cause diarrhoea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What long-term nutritional and GI side effects does colestyramine cause?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Constipation and bloating, plus malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, so long-term use may need vitamin supplementation.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How should other medicines be timed around colestyramine, and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Colestyramine binds other drugs in the gut (e.g. warfarin, digoxin, thyroxine, thiazides), reducing their absorption. Take other drugs 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after colestyramine to avoid this.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do aminosalicylates (5-ASA) such as mesalazine work in ulcerative colitis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They act topically on the gut mucosa to produce a local anti-inflammatory effect, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines and prostaglandins/leukotrienes. The action is on the mucosal surface rather than systemic.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the first-line drug class to both induce AND maintain remission in ulcerative colitis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Aminosalicylates (5-ASA, e.g. mesalazine, sulfasalazine). They are first-line for inducing and maintaining remission in UC.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In distal UC/proctitis, what is the stepwise use of 5-ASA before adding a steroid?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Start topical (rectal) 5-ASA first for proctitis/distal disease -> add oral 5-ASA -> add an oral steroid only if response is inadequate at 4 weeks.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Are aminosalicylates (5-ASA) effective in Crohn's disease?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No. They have no role in maintaining remission (ineffective) and only marginal/unproven value in induction. 5-ASAs are a UC drug, not a Crohn's drug.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on mesalazine develops rising creatinine/deranged U&Es. What serious adverse effect should you suspect, and what monitoring is required?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Interstitial nephritis. Monitor renal function (U&Es) at baseline and during treatment. 5-ASA can cause renal impairment via interstitial nephritis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on a 5-ASA reports unexplained bruising, bleeding or a sore throat. What should you do?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Suspect a blood dyscrasia (bone-marrow suppression). Stop and check an urgent FBC. Counsel patients to report unexplained bleeding, bruising or sore throat.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on mesalazine develops unexplained chest pain and breathlessness. What rare adverse effect must be considered?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Mesalazine-induced myocarditis/pericarditis (MHRA warning). Suspect it with unexplained chest pain, dyspnoea or arrhythmia, and stop the drug.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which 5-ASA is also used as a DMARD in rheumatoid and spondyloarthritis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Sulfasalazine. As well as its role in UC, it is used as a disease-modifying drug in rheumatoid/spondyloarthritis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A young man on sulfasalazine is worried about fertility. What reversible side effect should you counsel him about?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Reversible oligospermia causing male infertility. It resolves on stopping the drug. Consider switching to a non-sulfa 5-ASA if fertility is a concern.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient starting sulfasalazine notices orange-coloured urine and staining of soft contact lenses. Is this dangerous?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No — orange discolouration of urine and contact lenses is a harmless, expected effect of sulfasalazine. Reassure the patient.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is sulfasalazine hazardous in a patient with G6PD deficiency?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It can precipitate haemolysis (haemolytic anaemia) in G6PD deficiency. Sulfasalazine also impairs folate absorption, so folate may need monitoring/supplementation.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which vitamin's absorption is impaired by sulfasalazine, and what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Folate absorption is impaired. Monitor folate (and LFTs, as sulfasalazine can be hepatotoxic), and supplement if needed.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why must FBC be monitored closely when a 5-ASA (mesalazine/sulfasalazine) is combined with azathioprine or mercaptopurine?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: 5-ASAs increase the myelosuppressive effect of azathioprine/mercaptopurine (they inhibit TPMT), raising the risk of bone-marrow suppression. Monitor FBC closely.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the role of corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone) in IBD, and why are they NOT used long-term?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They rapidly induce remission in an acute IBD flare but are not used for maintenance because of their side-effect burden (Cushingoid effects, osteoporosis, diabetes, infection, adrenal suppression).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does budesonide cause fewer systemic side effects than prednisolone in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Budesonide is gut-targeted and undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, giving high gut-mucosal exposure but low systemic bioavailability. It is used for ileocaecal Crohn's and microscopic colitis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which corticosteroid regimen is used for acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: IV hydrocortisone (e.g. 100 mg QDS). It is given as part of the ASUC bundle with VTE prophylaxis, stool charting, daily CRP and day-3 response assessment.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In acute severe UC, should VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) be withheld because of the bloody diarrhoea?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No. ASUC is a prothrombotic state, so LMWH VTE prophylaxis should be given, NOT withheld, despite rectal bleeding.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: When is response to IV steroids assessed in acute severe UC, and what predicts likely colectomy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: At day 3. Poor response — e.g. >8 stools/day, or 3-8 stools/day with CRP >45 — predicts a high likelihood of needing colectomy. This triggers early surgical review and rescue therapy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the rescue (second-line) medical therapies if IV steroids fail in acute severe UC?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Infliximab OR ciclosporin, alongside early surgical review. These are given when day-3 assessment shows the patient is failing steroid therapy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why must corticosteroids never be stopped abruptly after a prolonged course?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Chronic steroids cause adrenal suppression; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Taper the dose, and provide an NHS Steroid Emergency Card with sick-day rules.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Name the key systemic adverse effects of corticosteroids a student should recognise.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cushingoid appearance, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, weight gain, hypertension, mood change/psychosis, immunosuppression/infection and adrenal suppression. Monitor glucose, BP and provide bone protection on prolonged/repeated courses.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why should live vaccines be avoided in patients on immunosuppressive doses of corticosteroids?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Immunosuppression means a live vaccine could cause disseminated infection. Live vaccines are contraindicated in significantly immunosuppressed patients.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the role of thiopurines (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine) in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are steroid-sparing immunosuppressants used to MAINTAIN remission in IBD. Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which is activated to metabolites that suppress proliferating lymphocytes.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which enzyme activities must be checked BEFORE starting azathioprine or mercaptopurine, and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: TPMT and NUDT15. Low/absent activity shunts the drug to toxic metabolites, causing severe, potentially fatal myelosuppression. Test both before starting and use activity to guide dosing.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the main dose-limiting and long-term risks of thiopurines, and how are they monitored?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Dose-limiting bone-marrow suppression (regular FBC), plus hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis and increased infection risk. Long-term there is an increased risk of lymphoma and non-melanoma skin cancer — advise sun protection. Monitor FBC and LFTs.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is co-prescribing allopurinol (or febuxostat) with azathioprine dangerous?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They block xanthine oxidase, massively increasing active thiopurine metabolites and causing life-threatening myelosuppression. Avoid the combination; if allopurinol is essential, cut the thiopurine to 25% (one-quarter) dose with intensified FBC monitoring.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is methotrexate used for in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Maintaining remission in Crohn's disease, especially in patients who are intolerant of thiopurines. (It is also used in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis.)

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is methotrexate dosed for Crohn's maintenance, and what fatal error must be avoided?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is given ONCE WEEKLY (e.g. 15-25 mg SC/PO), never daily — daily dosing is fatal. Folic acid is given on a DIFFERENT day of the week to reduce toxicity.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does low-dose weekly methotrexate exert its anti-inflammatory effect?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Mainly via an adenosine-mediated anti-inflammatory action (folate-antagonist/dihydrofolate reductase inhibition dominates only at high cytotoxic doses).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on methotrexate develops a new dry cough and breathlessness. What must you consider and do?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Methotrexate pneumonitis. Stop the drug and investigate. It is a potentially serious pulmonary toxicity presenting with dry cough and dyspnoea.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What must both male and female patients be counselled about regarding methotrexate and pregnancy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Methotrexate is teratogenic and abortifacient. Effective contraception is needed during treatment and for at least 6 months after stopping, in both sexes.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why must trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole be avoided in a patient taking methotrexate?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Both are antifolates, so combining them causes additive bone-marrow toxicity (severe myelosuppression). Avoid the combination. NSAIDs and PPIs also reduce methotrexate excretion and raise its levels.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What routine blood monitoring is required for a patient on methotrexate?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Regular FBC (marrow suppression), LFTs (hepatotoxicity/fibrosis) and U&Es (renal excretion). Also ensure pregnancy avoidance and advise reporting cough/dyspnoea (pneumonitis) and mouth ulcers (folate-responsive mucositis).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the mechanism of action of the anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab) in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are monoclonal antibodies against TNF-alpha -> they neutralise this key pro-inflammatory cytokine -> potent control of moderate-to-severe inflammatory bowel disease.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: For which IBD indications are anti-TNF biologics used?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Moderate-to-severe or refractory Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, fistulising Crohn's disease, and acute severe UC not responding to IV steroids.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which anti-TNF drug is the rescue therapy for acute severe UC not responding to IV steroids, and what is the alternative?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Infliximab is the anti-TNF rescue therapy. Ciclosporin is the alternative rescue agent.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Before starting an anti-TNF biologic, which latent infections must you screen for and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B (also hepatitis C and HIV). TNF-alpha maintains granuloma integrity, so anti-TNF therapy can reactivate latent TB; hepatitis B can also reactivate.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why can anti-TNF therapy reactivate latent tuberculosis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: TNF-alpha maintains granuloma integrity that walls off latent TB -> blocking TNF-alpha breaks down the granuloma -> latent TB reactivates. This is why TB screening is mandatory before starting.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which cardiac condition is a contraindication to anti-TNF biologics?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Moderate-to-severe heart failure -> anti-TNF therapy worsens it. Anti-TNF should also be avoided in demyelinating disease.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is infliximab often co-prescribed with a thiopurine or methotrexate?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Infliximab is chimeric (mouse/human) -> immunogenic -> patients form anti-drug antibodies causing secondary loss of response and infusion reactions. Combining with a thiopurine or methotrexate reduces immunogenicity and maintains response.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do the anti-TNF agents differ in immunogenicity and route?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Infliximab is chimeric and IV (more immunogenic). Adalimumab and golimumab are fully human and given SC (less immunogenic). Certolizumab is a PEGylated Fab' fragment with no Fc portion.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the typical induction and maintenance schedule for infliximab in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Infliximab 5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2 and 6, then 8-weekly maintenance. Adalimumab by contrast is given SC fortnightly.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the key malignancy and infection risks of anti-TNF biologics?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Increased risk of serious and opportunistic infections (including reactivated TB and hepatitis B), and an increased risk of lymphoma and skin cancer. Annual skin checks are advised; drug-induced lupus can also occur.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Can live vaccines be given during anti-TNF therapy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: No. Live vaccines are contraindicated during immunosuppression -> they must be given before starting the biologic. Also never combine two biologics due to serious infection risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the mechanism of action of vedolizumab in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a monoclonal antibody against alpha4beta7 integrin -> blocks its binding to MAdCAM-1 on gut endothelium -> stops lymphocyte homing specifically to the gut -> gut-selective immunosuppression.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does vedolizumab have a favourable systemic safety profile?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Its action is gut-selective (blocks alpha4beta7-MAdCAM-1 lymphocyte homing to the gut only) -> less systemic immunosuppression -> lower systemic infection risk. This makes it a good choice when systemic infection risk is a concern.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why does vedolizumab, unlike natalizumab, carry no meaningful risk of PML?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Natalizumab is anti-alpha4 and non-selective -> it blocks lymphocyte entry into the CNS -> risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) from JC virus. Vedolizumab's beta7 selectivity keeps its action gut-specific, so it carries no meaningful PML risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the main indications for vedolizumab?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, especially where you want to avoid systemic immunosuppression because of infection risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What safety screening and vaccine precautions apply to vedolizumab?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Still screen for latent TB before starting and watch for infection. Avoid live vaccines during treatment (immunosuppression).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the target of ustekinumab in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a monoclonal antibody to the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23 -> blocks these pro-inflammatory cytokines driving IBD.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the indications for ustekinumab, and how is it tolerated?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (also used in psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis). It is generally well tolerated; screen for TB before starting and avoid live vaccines.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is ustekinumab administered?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: IV weight-based induction dose, then SC maintenance every 8-12 weeks.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the mechanism of the IL-23 inhibitors risankizumab and mirikizumab, and how does it differ from ustekinumab?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are monoclonal antibodies to the p19 subunit of IL-23 -> selectively block IL-23 while sparing IL-12. Ustekinumab targets the shared p40 subunit, blocking both IL-12 and IL-23; the p19 agents are IL-23-selective.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which IBD indications are risankizumab and mirikizumab used for?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Risankizumab for moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease and mirikizumab for ulcerative colitis. They are newer, targeted, well-tolerated additions to the biologic ladder; screen for TB and avoid live vaccines.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib) differ from the IBD biologics in class and route?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They are oral small-molecule Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, not injectable biologics -> they block JAK-STAT signalling downstream of multiple cytokine receptors -> immunosuppression. Being oral, they offer a rapid oral treatment option.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the indications for JAK inhibitors in IBD?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (upadacitinib is also used in Crohn's disease), often after biologic failure. They provide a rapid oral option.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the MHRA class safety flags for JAK inhibitors?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation (characteristic), venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE), raised lipids, and an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In which patients does the MHRA advise particular caution with JAK inhibitors, and how are they restricted?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: JAK inhibitors are restricted to when other treatment options are unsuitable, with particular caution in patients over 65, smokers, and those with cardiovascular or cancer risk.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which characteristic infective side effect should prompt vaccination consideration before starting a JAK inhibitor?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation is characteristic -> consider zoster vaccination before starting. Give any live vaccines before starting (contraindicated during treatment) and screen for TB and hepatitis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What monitoring is needed for a patient on a JAK inhibitor for UC?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Monitor FBC, lipids and LFTs, and assess VTE and cardiovascular risk. Watch for infection and cytopenias; screen for TB/hepatitis before starting.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is a typical dosing pattern for tofacitinib and upadacitinib in ulcerative colitis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily induction, then 5 mg twice daily maintenance. Upadacitinib 45 mg once daily induction, then 15-30 mg once daily maintenance (filgotinib 200 mg once daily).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In the IBD biologic ladder, which agent is the most gut-selective and systemically safest, and which classes carry more systemic risk?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Vedolizumab is gut-selective and has the most favourable systemic safety profile (safest systemically).
