pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Active malignancy and acute critical illness (increases mortality); also active intracranial hypertension and proliferative diabetic retinopathy. In Prader-Willi, screen for severe obesity/OSA first (sudden-death risk).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do glucocorticoids (e.g. prednisolone, dexamethasone) produce their anti-inflammatory effect at the cellular level?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They bind intracellular glucocorticoid receptors and alter gene transcription, reducing cytokine production and leukocyte activity. This gives broad anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, alongside metabolic effects (raised glucose, protein catabolism, fat redistribution).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Name three broad categories of condition where systemic corticosteroids are used.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Acute inflammatory/allergic states (asthma/COPD exacerbations, anaphylaxis, allergy), autoimmune/inflammatory disease (RA, PMR/GCA, vasculitis, IBD, SLE) and transplant immunosuppression. Also cerebral oedema (dexamethasone) and adrenal replacement (hydrocortisone).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What three properties differ between the systemic corticosteroids and determine which one you choose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Potency, duration of action, and mineralocorticoid (sodium/fluid-retaining) activity. For example dexamethasone is high-potency, long-acting with negligible mineralocorticoid effect, whereas hydrocortisone is low-potency with more mineralocorticoid activity.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Rank hydrocortisone, prednisolone and dexamethasone by anti-inflammatory potency.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hydrocortisone (potency 1) -> prednisolone (~4) -> methylprednisolone (~5) -> dexamethasone/betamethasone (~25-30). The higher-potency steroids are also longer-acting with negligible mineralocorticoid activity.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which systemic corticosteroid is used for cerebral oedema, and why is it well suited?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dexamethasone. It is high-potency, long-acting and has negligible mineralocorticoid (sodium/fluid-retaining) activity, so it reduces oedema without causing fluid retention.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which corticosteroid is typically used for physiological adrenal replacement, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hydrocortisone. It most closely mimics endogenous cortisol, having both glucocorticoid and useful mineralocorticoid activity at replacement doses.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: At what time of day should a once-daily corticosteroid be given, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: In the morning. This mimics the natural diurnal cortisol rhythm, reducing insomnia and minimising suppression of the HPA (adrenal) axis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: List the situations where a corticosteroid course must be withdrawn gradually (tapered) rather than stopped abruptly.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Taper if: used for more than 3 weeks, dose above 40 mg prednisolone-equivalent, repeated courses, evening dosing, or a further course given within 1 year of stopping long-term therapy.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What does the 'STEROIDS' mnemonic stand for as a list of corticosteroid side effects?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Stomach ulcers, Thin skin/easy bruising, oEdema, Right & left heart failure, Osteoporosis, Infection (immunosuppression), Diabetes/hyperglycaemia, Syndrome (Cushingoid appearance) + weight gain.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Beyond the STEROIDS mnemonic, name several other important corticosteroid adverse effects.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Mood change/psychosis, cataracts and glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy, proximal myopathy, avascular necrosis, growth retardation in children, and adrenal suppression.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient on long-term steroids reports new blurred vision. What serious eye side effect must you consider, and what is the advice?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Central serous chorioretinopathy (fluid under the retina). The MHRA advises that any patient on steroids by ANY route reporting blurred vision should be referred/assessed, as this can occur with all routes of administration.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: At what doses can serious psychiatric reactions to corticosteroids occur?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: At ANY dose, and even on withdrawal. The MHRA warns of depression, suicidal ideation, mania and psychosis; warn patients and act promptly if mood or behaviour changes.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why must long-term systemic steroids never be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They suppress the HPA axis, so the adrenal glands cannot immediately produce cortisol. Abrupt withdrawal risks an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis. The dose must be tapered gradually.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What should a patient on long-term steroids be given/carry to protect against adrenal crisis?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: The red NHS Steroid Emergency Card (2020), plus counselling on sick-day rules (increase the dose during illness) and the need for extra steroid cover around surgery. They should also carry a blue steroid treatment card.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are 'sick-day rules' for a patient on long-term corticosteroids?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: During acute illness, fever or physiological stress the patient must increase (e.g. double) their steroid dose to match the extra cortisol the body would normally produce, preventing adrenal crisis. They may need parenteral hydrocortisone if vomiting.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What bone protection should be considered for a patient starting a prolonged corticosteroid course?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A bisphosphonate plus calcium and vitamin D, to counter steroid-induced osteoporosis. Prolonged steroids markedly increase fracture risk.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why co-prescribe a PPI when a patient is on both a corticosteroid and an NSAID?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Steroids and NSAIDs each raise peptic ulcer/GI bleed risk, and together the risk is markedly increased. Gastroprotection with a PPI is used to reduce this.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do corticosteroids affect blood glucose, and what is the implication for a diabetic patient?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Steroids raise blood glucose. A diabetic patient will usually need increased antidiabetic therapy, and non-diabetics may develop steroid-induced hyperglycaemia; monitor glucose.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do enzyme inducers such as rifampicin or phenytoin affect corticosteroid therapy?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They increase steroid metabolism and reduce steroid levels, which can lead to loss of therapeutic effect (or precipitate under-replacement). The steroid dose may need increasing.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is combining a corticosteroid with a diuretic potentially dangerous, especially in a patient on digoxin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Both cause potassium loss, so together they potentiate hypokalaemia. Low K+ increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which vaccines are contraindicated in a patient on immunosuppressive doses of corticosteroids?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Live vaccines. Because steroids suppress immunity, live vaccines risk causing disseminated infection and should be avoided while immunosuppressed.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What routine parameters should be monitored during a prolonged corticosteroid course?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Blood glucose, blood pressure and weight. Also consider bone protection, gastroprotection, and watching for mood change, infection and eye problems.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why should systemic corticosteroids be used with caution in a patient with active systemic infection?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Their immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory action can mask signs of infection and allow it to worsen or disseminate. Existing infection should be treated/controlled and the patient monitored closely.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient with a peptic ulcer history and a psychiatric history needs a steroid course. What cautions apply?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Steroids can reactivate/worsen peptic ulcers (consider gastroprotection) and can trigger serious mood disturbance or psychosis at any dose. Use with caution, warn the patient, and monitor. Similar caution applies with diabetes, osteoporosis and hypertension.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the drug of choice for treating hypokalaemia, and how is the route chosen?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Potassium chloride. Oral (e.g. Sando-K/Kay-Cee-L) for mild hypokalaemia or maintenance; IV KCl for moderate-severe or symptomatic hypokalaemia (arrhythmia, weakness).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A patient with hypokalaemia keeps having a low K+ despite repeated potassium replacement. What must you check and correct?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Serum magnesium. Hypokalaemia is refractory and won't rise until a low magnesium is corrected -> always replace Mg2+ alongside K+.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why must IV potassium chloride NEVER be given as a bolus or 'push'?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: A rapid rise in serum K+ causes a fatal arrhythmia/cardiac arrest. IV potassium must always be diluted and infused slowly, never pushed.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What are the maximum safe concentration and rate for IV potassium given through a peripheral line?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Max concentration 40 mmol/L and max rate 10 mmol/h. Faster infusion requires cardiac monitoring and central venous access.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why are concentrated potassium chloride ampoules classed as a 'Never Event', and how should IV potassium be supplied?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Accidental IV administration of concentrated KCl is fatal, so it is a Never Event. Concentrated ampoules are removed from general ward stock -> use pre-diluted/ready-made infusion bags only.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which drug classes cause additive hyperkalaemia and should not be co-prescribed with potassium supplements unless closely monitored?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone/eplerenone/amiloride), ACE inhibitors/ARBs, trimethoprim, ciclosporin/tacrolimus and NSAIDs.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What monitoring is required during IV potassium chloride replacement?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Serial U&Es and ECG during the infusion, plus checking and correcting magnesium. Faster or central infusions require continuous cardiac monitoring.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Besides fatal arrhythmia, what local side effects can IV or oral potassium cause?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: IV: phlebitis and pain at the peripheral infusion site. Oral: GI irritation.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How is hyperkalaemia graded by severity in mmol/L?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Mild 5.5-5.9, moderate 6.0-6.4, severe >=6.5 mmol/L.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: When should hyperkalaemia be treated urgently as an emergency?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: If there are ECG changes, or if K+ >=6.5 mmol/L -> requires immediate treatment.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the FIRST drug given in hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, and what does it do?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Calcium gluconate. It raises the myocyte threshold potential -> stabilises the myocardium against the arrhythmogenic effect of high K+. It does NOT lower serum potassium.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How quickly does calcium gluconate work in hyperkalaemia, and how long does it last?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Fast onset (~1-3 min) but short-lived (~30-60 min). Repeat the dose if ECG changes persist.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A patient with hyperkalaemia and ECG changes is on digoxin. Why is calcium gluconate dangerous here?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: In digoxin toxicity, calcium can precipitate a fatal arrhythmia ('stone heart'). Give slowly and cautiously (or avoid) with cardiac monitoring.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why must IV calcium and IV sodium bicarbonate never be given through the same line?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: They precipitate as calcium carbonate. Use separate lines or flush with 0.9% saline between them.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Aside from hyperkalaemia, what are the main indications for IV calcium gluconate?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany/seizures), as the antidote for magnesium toxicity, and in calcium-channel-blocker overdose.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the standard dose of calcium gluconate in hyperkalaemia with ECG changes?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV, cardiac-monitored, repeated as needed if ECG changes persist.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the main potassium-SHIFTING treatment in hyperkalaemia, and how does it work?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Insulin with dextrose. Insulin drives K+ into cells (stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase), temporarily lowering serum potassium; dextrose is co-given to prevent hypoglycaemia.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is a typical insulin-dextrose regimen for hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: 10 units of soluble insulin in 25 g glucose IV over ~15-30 min. Write 'units' in full and draw up the insulin with an insulin syringe.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: After giving insulin-dextrose for hyperkalaemia, what is the key monitoring requirement and why?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Monitor capillary glucose for at least 6 hours, because of delayed hypoglycaemia - especially in CKD, low-weight or non-diabetic patients.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Does insulin-dextrose remove potassium from the body in hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: No - it only SHIFTS K+ into cells to buy time. Definitive removal (a potassium binder, diuresis or dialysis) must still be arranged.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the role of nebulised salbutamol in hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: A beta-2 agonist that also drives K+ into cells -> an ADD-ON to insulin-dextrose for extra potassium lowering. It is not used as the sole shifting agent and is less reliable than insulin-dextrose.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What dose of nebulised salbutamol is used in hyperkalaemia, and how does it compare with the asthma dose?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised - a much higher dose than used for asthma.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What side effects limit the use of high-dose nebulised salbutamol, and in whom is it a particular caution?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Tachycardia, tremor and palpitations. Caution in ischaemic heart disease and tachyarrhythmias.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: In hyperkalaemia, when is sodium bicarbonate used, and why is it not part of the core shift therapy?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Only if the patient is acidotic. Acidosis drives K+ out of cells, so buffering H+ helps shift K+ back in - but it is a slow, weak shifter and is NOT part of the standard insulin/salbutamol therapy.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Sodium bicarbonate is used to alkalinise urine/plasma in which two classic overdoses?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Aspirin (salicylate) overdose and tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose (also used in rhabdomyolysis).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What are the main hazards of giving IV sodium bicarbonate?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Sodium and fluid overload, metabolic alkalosis, and a falling ionised calcium (-> tetany). Do not mix with IV calcium in the same line; concentrated (8.4%) solution causes necrosis on extravasation.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: When is ORAL sodium bicarbonate used?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: For metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease (e.g. NICE: eGFR <30 and bicarbonate <20 mmol/L).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the overall stabilise-shift-remove sequence for managing severe hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: (1) Calcium gluconate to protect/stabilise the heart if there are ECG changes; (2) insulin-dextrose (+/- nebulised salbutamol) to SHIFT K+ into cells; (3) a potassium binder or dialysis to REMOVE potassium from the body.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How do potassium binders (calcium resonium, patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) actually lower serum K+ — and how does this differ from insulin/salbutamol?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: They act in the gut, binding/exchanging K+ so it is excreted in the stool -> they REMOVE potassium from the body. This is definitive lowering, unlike insulin+glucose and salbutamol, which only SHIFT K+ into cells temporarily.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which potassium binder has a fast enough onset (~1 h) to help acutely lower K+, and which is only useful for chronic control?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) works within ~1 h and is the only binder with a role in acute lowering. Patiromer has a slow onset (~7 h) -> chronic/maintenance control only, not for emergencies.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Where do potassium binders fit in the management of hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: For chronic/persistent hyperkalaemia (e.g. CKD on ACEi/ARB) to remove K+, or after emergency shifting therapy (insulin/salbutamol/calcium) to definitively clear the potassium load. SZC can also assist acute lowering.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A patient on calcium resonium reports no bowel movement for several days. What is the risk and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Resonium commonly causes constipation and can cause faecal impaction (rarely intestinal/colonic necrosis, especially with sorbitol). Co-prescribe a laxative and monitor bowel function; avoid in bowel obstruction or reduced gut motility.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the key MHRA interaction warning for ALL oral potassium binders?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: They reduce absorption of other oral medicines. Give other oral drugs at least 3 hours before or after the binder to avoid reduced drug levels.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which potassium binder can cause hypomagnesaemia, and which can cause oedema?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Patiromer -> hypomagnesaemia (monitor Mg2+). SZC -> oedema from its sodium load (monitor fluid status/BP; caution in heart failure).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which monitoring is important when using potassium binders?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Serum K+ (watch for overshoot/hypokalaemia); Mg2+ with patiromer; fluid balance/oedema and BP with SZC; bowel function with calcium resonium.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the mechanism of IV magnesium sulphate as a therapy?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: It replaces magnesium and stabilises excitable membranes (myocardium, neuromuscular junction, bronchial and uterine smooth muscle). It is a cofactor for the Na+/K+-ATPase; in eclampsia it also acts as a cerebral vasodilator and reduces seizure activity.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What are the three classic emergency indications for IV magnesium sulphate?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Torsades de pointes (and VT/VF in hypomagnesaemia), severe/life-threatening asthma, and eclampsia/pre-eclampsia (seizure prophylaxis and treatment). It also treats hypomagnesaemia.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why does correcting hypomagnesaemia matter when treating hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Low Mg2+ perpetuates hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia — the K+ and Ca2+ are hard to correct until the magnesium is replaced. Always check and replace Mg2+ alongside them.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the IV magnesium sulphate regimen for eclampsia, and how long is it continued?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: 4 g IV loading dose (over ~5-15 min), then a 1 g/hour infusion, continued for 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure (whichever is later). A recurrent seizure is treated with a further 2-4 g bolus.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the earliest clinical sign of magnesium toxicity, and how do you monitor for it?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the early warning sign. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, BP and urine output during the infusion; a falling/absent reflex means stop the magnesium.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Magnesium toxicity progresses beyond areflexia to what, and what is the antidote?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: After loss of reflexes: respiratory depression, hypotension, then bradycardia/cardiac arrest. The antidote is IV calcium gluconate.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why must the IV magnesium sulphate dose be reduced/used with caution in severe renal impairment?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Magnesium is renally excreted, so impaired kidneys cause accumulation -> toxicity. Reduce the dose and monitor reflexes/levels closely (also caution in heart block).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the default crystalloid for fluid resuscitation and maintenance in a UK hospital?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: 0.9% sodium chloride (isotonic saline) — used as boluses (e.g. 250-500 mL) for resuscitation, and for maintenance at ~25-30 mL/kg/day (with added potassium). It is also a common vehicle for IV drugs.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What acid-base disturbance can result from giving large volumes of 0.9% saline, and what is the alternative?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis (from the high chloride load). Balanced crystalloids such as Hartmann's may be preferred for large-volume resuscitation.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Compare 0.9% and 0.45% sodium chloride — when is each used?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: 0.9% is isotonic — for volume/sodium replacement and resuscitation. 0.45% is hypotonic — provides more free water, used for free-water replacement. Both need caution in fluid overload/heart failure.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why must chronic hyponatraemia be corrected SLOWLY, and what is the safe rate?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Too-rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome. Limit the rise in serum Na+ to less than ~10 mmol/L per 24 h (less if high ODS risk), monitoring U&Es closely.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A patient has severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (e.g. seizures/reduced GCS). Which fluid is indicated — and not 0.9% saline?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hypertonic 3% saline (e.g. a 150 mL bolus), not 0.9% saline, to raise Na+ quickly enough to treat the emergency — while still capping the total 24 h rise to avoid osmotic demyelination.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which type of hyponatraemia is 0.9% saline used to correct?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia — restoring volume switches off ADH and allows the sodium to correct. (0.9% saline can worsen euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia such as SIADH.)

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How does tolvaptan work and what class is it?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: It is a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist ('vaptan'). It blocks ADH at the collecting duct -> aquaresis (water excreted without sodium) -> serum sodium rises.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What are the two main indications for tolvaptan?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hyponatraemia due to SIADH (and other euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia), and slowing cyst growth in ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why is tolvaptan started in hospital with frequent sodium monitoring?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Its aquaresis can raise serum Na+ too fast -> osmotic demyelination syndrome. Start in hospital, check sodium frequently, and limit the rise (roughly <8-10 mmol/L per 24 h); no fluid restriction on the first day.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which organ toxicity requires monitoring on tolvaptan, especially in ADPKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs (particularly with the higher doses used in ADPKD). Other common effects are thirst and polyuria.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which drugs raise tolvaptan levels, and what other therapies should be avoided alongside it?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Drugs that inhibit its metabolism (e.g. clarithromycin, grapefruit) raise its levels -> avoid. Also avoid combining with hypertonic saline or other hyponatraemia therapies, as they add up to an over-rapid sodium rise.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: In which patients is tolvaptan contraindicated?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia and anuria (it needs functioning kidneys to produce aquaresis, and volume-depleted patients would be harmed). Caution with hepatotoxicity risk.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Conceptually, why do potassium binders differ from emergency 'shift' therapies in a hyperkalaemia protocol?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Shift therapies (insulin+glucose, salbutamol) and calcium gluconate (cardioprotection) buy time but leave the total body K+ unchanged. Binders (and dialysis/diuresis) actually eliminate potassium — binders do so via the gut into stool.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why do patients with CKD develop anaemia, and what class of drug treats it?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: The failing kidney's peritubular cells make too little erythropoietin (EPO) -> reduced red-cell production -> anaemia of CKD. Recombinant erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) such as epoetin and darbepoetin replace the missing EPO and stimulate the marrow to make red cells.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How do epoetin and darbepoetin differ practically?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Both are recombinant erythropoietin that stimulate red-cell production. Darbepoetin is more heavily glycosylated -> longer duration of action -> can be given less frequently than epoetin.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Before starting or increasing an ESA for anaemia of CKD, what must you check first and why?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Ensure the patient is iron-replete (and B12/folate-replete). CKD raises hepcidin causing functional iron deficiency, and ESAs simply fail if iron-deficient. Correct iron first, then start/uptitrate the ESA.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What haemoglobin should you target when using an ESA in CKD, and why not aim for normal?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Titrate to a target Hb of roughly 100-120 g/L, NOT a normal level. Over-correcting Hb increases hypertension, thrombosis and stroke risk. Consider an ESA when Hb is <=100 g/L and the patient is symptomatic.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A CKD patient on epoetin develops severe headache, very high BP and a seizure. What ESA-related complication is this?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hypertension / hypertensive encephalopathy with seizures - a recognised ESA side effect. ESAs raise blood pressure; uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication and BP must be monitored and controlled.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A patient on an ESA suddenly loses their response and becomes transfusion-dependent with anti-EPO antibodies. What is the diagnosis and what must you NOT do?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Pure red-cell aplasia from anti-EPO antibodies. Stop the ESA and do NOT switch to a different ESA - they cross-react, so another ESA will also fail/be attacked.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What should you monitor in a CKD patient on an ESA?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Haemoglobin (avoid over-correction, keep ~100-120 g/L), blood pressure, and iron status (ferritin and transferrin saturation).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why is IV iron often preferred over oral iron in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: CKD inflammation raises hepcidin, which blocks gut iron absorption. Parenteral (IV) iron bypasses the gut, replenishes stores directly and supports erythropoiesis and the response to ESAs, where oral iron would be poorly absorbed.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the key safety requirement when giving IV iron, and how long must you observe afterwards?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: IV iron can cause anaphylaxis/hypersensitivity. Give it only where staff are trained in managing anaphylaxis with resuscitation facilities and adrenaline available, and observe the patient for at least 30 minutes after each dose. Test doses are NOT reliable.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why should IV iron be avoided in a patient with active infection or sepsis?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Free iron can worsen infection (bacteria use iron), so IV iron is avoided during active infection/sepsis and given once the infection has settled.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: A patient develops hypophosphataemia after repeated ferric carboxymaltose infusions. Is this expected?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Yes - ferric carboxymaltose (Ferinject) can cause hypophosphataemia. Check phosphate with repeated dosing.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What iron targets are you aiming for when treating iron deficiency in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Aim for transferrin saturation (TSAT) >20% and ferritin >100 micrograms/L (without over-loading - avoid very high ferritin). Recheck iron indices a few weeks after dosing.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How and when are oral phosphate binders taken, and what do they treat?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: They are taken WITH meals so they bind dietary phosphate in the gut and reduce its absorption, treating the hyperphosphataemia of CKD. Dietary phosphate restriction is tried first, then a binder is added.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: When would you choose a non-calcium phosphate binder (sevelamer or lanthanum) over a calcium-based one?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: When calcium is high or you want to limit total calcium load. Calcium-based binders (calcium carbonate/acetate) risk hypercalcaemia and vascular calcification, so non-calcium binders like sevelamer or lanthanum are preferred in those situations.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What extra properties distinguish sevelamer and lanthanum as phosphate binders?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Sevelamer is a non-absorbed binder that also lowers LDL cholesterol and adds no calcium load. Lanthanum is radio-opaque, so it can appear on X-rays. Both avoid the calcium load of calcium-based binders.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why must other oral medicines be separated from phosphate binder doses?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Binders reduce the gut absorption of many co-administered oral drugs - e.g. levothyroxine, quinolone/tetracycline antibiotics, bisphosphonates, oral iron and digoxin - so these should be taken at a different time from the binder.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is monitored in a CKD patient on phosphate binders?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Serum phosphate, calcium and PTH. (And ensure the binder is taken with meals for it to work.)

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why are alfacalcidol and calcitriol given instead of ordinary vitamin D in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: The diseased kidney cannot perform the final activation (1-alpha-hydroxylation) of vitamin D, so active forms (alfacalcidol/calcitriol) are given already activated. They raise calcium absorption and suppress PTH, treating secondary (renal) hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why should phosphate be controlled before starting active vitamin D in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Active vitamin D raises both calcium and phosphate absorption. Starting it with uncontrolled phosphate worsens hyperphosphataemia and promotes vascular calcification, so control phosphate (diet + binders) first.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What are the main risks of active vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol) in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia (-> vascular calcification), and over-suppression of PTH -> adynamic bone disease. Titrate to calcium and PTH, monitoring calcium, phosphate and PTH.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Why is combining active vitamin D with a calcium-based phosphate binder a hypercalcaemia risk?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Both raise serum calcium, so the effect is additive -> greater risk of hypercalcaemia. Monitor calcium; a non-calcium binder may be preferred if calcium is a concern.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: How does cinacalcet lower PTH, and what type of drug is it?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic: it binds the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor and makes it more sensitive to calcium, so the gland behaves as if calcium is higher -> reduced PTH secretion (and lower calcium).

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the key advantage of cinacalcet over active vitamin D for lowering PTH?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Cinacalcet lowers PTH (and calcium) WITHOUT raising calcium and phosphate, whereas active vitamin D raises them. This makes it useful when calcium/phosphate are already high.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: When is cinacalcet used in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: For refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism in dialysis patients when parathyroidectomy is contraindicated or inappropriate (after diet, phosphate binders and active vitamin D have failed). It is also used in parathyroid carcinoma.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the main danger of cinacalcet, and when must you NOT start it?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Hypocalcaemia - which can cause paraesthesia, cramps, QT prolongation and seizures. Do NOT start cinacalcet if corrected calcium is below the normal range. Check corrected calcium within 1 week of starting or changing the dose, plus PTH.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Which interaction concept should you remember for cinacalcet?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Cinacalcet can raise the levels of some other drugs, such as metoprolol, tricyclic antidepressants and flecainide (narrow therapeutic index) - these may need dose reduction or monitoring.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What problem does oral sodium bicarbonate correct in CKD, and what benefit may it give?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: It corrects the chronic metabolic acidosis of CKD (failing kidneys can't excrete acid). Normalising bicarbonate may slow CKD progression and protect bone and muscle.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: Per NICE, when should oral sodium bicarbonate be offered in CKD?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: When eGFR is <30 mL/min AND serum bicarbonate is <20 mmol/L, titrating the dose to normalise the serum bicarbonate.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is the main downside of oral sodium bicarbonate, and in whom is caution needed?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: It delivers a sodium/fluid load -> fluid retention, oedema and hypertension. Use with caution in heart failure. Monitor serum bicarbonate, BP and fluid status; over-correction can cause alkalosis.

pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.front: What is CKD mineral-bone disorder (CKD-MBD) and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Renal & Electrolyte Drugs_.back: Phosphate retention and reduced active vitamin D in CKD drive secondary hyperparathyroidism and bone/vascular disease. Management: dietary phosphate restriction + phosphate binders + active vitamin D, with cinacalcet added for refractory cases, aiming to control phosphate, calcium and PTH.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do SSRIs work, and why is the antidepressant benefit not seen immediately?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They selectively block serotonin (5-HT) reuptake, so synaptic 5-HT rises straight away, but the clinical benefit is delayed by about 2-4 weeks (it needs adaptive changes to develop). The early weeks can transiently worsen anxiety before the mood benefit appears.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for depression and for most anxiety disorders (GAD, panic, OCD, PTSD)?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An SSRI. They are preferred because they have fewer antimuscarinic and cardiac effects than TCAs. In less-severe depression, do not default to a drug first -> offer psychological therapy/guided self-help.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which SSRI is preferred in a patient with recent MI or established cardiac disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sertraline - it has the cleanest interaction profile and the best safety evidence post-MI.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which antidepressant is first-line in an under-18 with depression, and what must accompany it?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Fluoxetine, and only alongside psychological therapy (with CAMHS input). Drug treatment alone is not appropriate in this age group.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why do citalopram and escitalopram carry dose caps, and who needs a lower maximum?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They prolong the QT interval. Dose is capped (citalopram max 40 mg; escitalopram max 20 mg), with a lower maximum in the elderly (>65) and in hepatic impairment (citalopram 20 mg / escitalopram 10 mg). Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs and correct low K+/Mg2+.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A young patient is started on an SSRI. When should they be reviewed, and why is the first few weeks a high-risk period?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Review at 2 weeks - but within 1 week if under 30 or at high suicide risk. There is a transient increase in anxiety, agitation and suicidal ideation in the first weeks, especially in the under-30s, before the mood benefit develops.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Once a patient has responded to an SSRI, how long should treatment be continued?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: For at least 6 months after remission (longer, e.g. 2 years, if recurrent depression), to reduce relapse risk. Do not stop as soon as they feel better.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the common early side effects and the key longer-term side effect that patients should be warned about with SSRIs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Early: GI upset/nausea and headache, plus a transient rise in anxiety. Ongoing: sexual dysfunction (very common and a frequent reason for non-adherence).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: An elderly patient on an SSRI becomes confused with a low sodium. What is the likely cause?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyponatraemia due to SIADH - a recognised SSRI effect, particularly in the elderly. Check sodium if symptoms of hyponatraemia develop.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on an SSRI also needs an NSAID (or is on an anticoagulant). What is the risk and what should be co-prescribed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: SSRIs increase the risk of GI bleeding, which is compounded by NSAIDs/anticoagulants. Add a PPI for gastroprotection.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should an SSRI never be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Abrupt cessation causes a discontinuation syndrome (flu-like symptoms, dizziness, electric-shock sensations, anxiety, sleep disturbance). Taper the dose gradually to stop. Paroxetine has the worst discontinuation syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A woman with breast cancer on tamoxifen needs an antidepressant. Which SSRIs are best avoided, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Avoid fluoxetine and paroxetine - they reduce the activation of tamoxifen (a prodrug) and so reduce its efficacy. Choose an alternative such as sertraline.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What washout is required when switching between an SSRI and an MAOI, and why is fluoxetine different?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Allow a 2-week washout to avoid serotonin syndrome - but 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine, because of its long duration of action.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) differ mechanistically from SSRIs, and where do they sit in therapy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They block reuptake of both serotonin AND noradrenaline. They are used second-line, typically as a switch after an SSRI has not worked (chosen on individual factors, not severity).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which antidepressant is used for diabetic/peripheral neuropathic pain as well as depression?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Duloxetine (an SNRI). It is licensed for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (and also stress incontinence).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What dose-related side effect must you monitor for with venlafaxine, and what is the monitoring?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Dose-related hypertension - the noradrenergic effect emerges at higher doses. Check blood pressure, especially as the dose is increased.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides hypertension, what two safety concerns are important with venlafaxine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A marked discontinuation syndrome (short-acting -> taper carefully to stop) and cardiotoxicity in overdose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do TCAs cause their characteristic side effects, beyond their effect on serotonin and noradrenaline?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As well as blocking serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake they block muscarinic, histamine (H1) and alpha-1 receptors -> antimuscarinic effects, sedation/weight gain and postural hypotension. They also block cardiac Na+ channels, which drives their overdose toxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the main modern use of TCAs such as amitriptyline, and how does the dose compare to antidepressant dosing?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Mainly low-dose for neuropathic/chronic pain, migraine prophylaxis and to aid sleep - e.g. amitriptyline 10-25 mg at night, much lower than the antidepressant dose of 75-150 mg.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What antimuscarinic side effects should you warn a patient about when starting a TCA?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and blurred vision. Also expect sedation, weight gain and postural hypotension.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient has taken a TCA overdose with a widened QRS, arrhythmia and seizures. What is the specific treatment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: IV sodium bicarbonate - the sodium load plus alkalinisation displaces the drug from cardiac Na+ channels, narrowing the QRS. TCA overdose is a common fatal overdose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should TCA prescribing be modified in a patient with suicide risk, and which agents matter here?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Prescribe limited quantities because TCAs are very dangerous in overdose. Lofepramine is the safest in overdose; dosulepin and amitriptyline are the most dangerous.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which cardiac situations are TCAs contraindicated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Recent MI, arrhythmias and heart block (they block cardiac Na+ channels). Also avoid in mania and use caution in severe prostatism/glaucoma.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do MAOIs work, and where do they sit in the treatment of depression?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They inhibit monoamine oxidase, reducing breakdown of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine. They are last-line/specialist agents for treatment-resistant or atypical depression, largely superseded by safer drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the MAOI 'cheese reaction' and what triggers it?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A hypertensive crisis. Tyramine (normally broken down in the gut) from tyramine-rich foods - mature cheese, cured meat, Marmite, red wine - or from sympathomimetics is absorbed and displaces stored noradrenaline -> severe hypertension. Patients need strict dietary restriction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is moclobemide considered much safer than phenelzine or tranylcypromine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Moclobemide is a reversible inhibitor (RIMA) - it is displaced by a tyramine surge, so it usually needs no dietary restriction. Phenelzine and tranylcypromine are irreversible and carry the full cheese-reaction and washout risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What washout periods apply when switching an SSRI to an MAOI (and vice versa)?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Strict washouts are needed to avoid serotonin syndrome: typically 2 weeks, but 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine. After stopping an irreversible MAOI, wait 2 weeks before starting an SSRI/SNRI/TCA.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does serotonin syndrome present?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A triad of altered mental state (agitation), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating) and neuromuscular excitability (tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which drug combinations should make you think of serotonin syndrome?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Combining serotonergic drugs - e.g. SSRIs/SNRIs plus an MAOI, linezolid, triptans, tramadol/pethidine, methylene blue or St John's Wort. Manage by stopping the offending drugs and giving supportive care.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What class of antidepressant is mirtazapine, and how does its mechanism differ from an SSRI?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA). It blocks presynaptic alpha-2 receptors (-> increased noradrenaline and serotonin release) and blocks histamine and some serotonin (5-HT2/5-HT3) receptors -> sedating and appetite-stimulating, with less nausea and sexual dysfunction than SSRIs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A depressed elderly patient has prominent insomnia and weight loss. Which antidepressant is particularly suited to this presentation, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Mirtazapine. It is sedating (helps insomnia) and appetite-stimulating (helps poor appetite/weight loss), making it a good choice where insomnia and weight loss dominate, e.g. in the elderly or cachexia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: At what time of day is mirtazapine taken, and what is the counter-intuitive dose-response for its sedative effect?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Taken at night (nocte). Paradoxically it is MORE sedating at LOWER doses, because the antihistamine effect dominates at low dose; higher noradrenergic activity at higher doses can be less sedating.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which side effects of mirtazapine are often used therapeutically, and how does its sexual/GI side-effect profile compare with SSRIs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation and increased appetite/weight gain are often used to the patient's advantage (insomnia, poor appetite). It causes fewer GI and sexual side effects than SSRIs. Dry mouth also occurs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on mirtazapine develops fever, sore throat and signs of infection. What rare adverse effect must you consider, and what do you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Agranulocytosis (a blood dyscrasia). Perform an urgent FBC and stop mirtazapine if a blood dyscrasia is confirmed. Warn patients to report sore throat, fever or infection.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of bupropion, and why does it lack sexual side effects?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI). It has little serotonergic effect, so it does not cause the sexual dysfunction typical of SSRIs; it also reduces nicotine craving and withdrawal.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the only UK-licensed indication for bupropion?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Smoking cessation. Unlike in the US, it is not licensed or NICE-recommended for depression in the UK.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When is bupropion started relative to a patient's planned quit date for smoking cessation?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is started 1-2 weeks BEFORE the target quit date, then continued afterwards.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key safety caution with bupropion, and which conditions therefore contraindicate it?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It lowers the seizure threshold. It is contraindicated in epilepsy/seizure disorder, eating disorders, and alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal (all of which further increase seizure risk).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which antidepressant class must never be combined with bupropion?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: MAOIs - bupropion is contraindicated with MAOIs, and an adequate washout period is required. Additive risk also occurs with other drugs that lower the seizure threshold.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What does it mean that vortioxetine is a 'multimodal' serotonergic antidepressant, and when is it used?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It acts on serotonin in several ways at once (reuptake inhibition plus actions at multiple serotonin receptors). It is an option in major depression, including where cognitive symptoms are prominent, when other antidepressants are unsuitable or ineffective.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the most common side effect of vortioxetine, and how does its sexual side-effect profile compare with SSRIs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Nausea is common. It causes fewer sexual side effects than SSRIs, but shares the serotonin syndrome and bleeding risks of other serotonergic drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What washout and interaction cautions apply to vortioxetine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An MAOI washout is required. Combining it with other serotonergic drugs (e.g. triptans, tramadol, linezolid) risks serotonin syndrome, and like other serotonergics it can increase bleeding risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of agomelatine, and what is its main clinical benefit?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a melatonin-receptor agonist (with a serotonin action) that resynchronises circadian rhythm and improves sleep. It is used in major depression, particularly where sleep disturbance is prominent, with few sexual side effects and no discontinuation syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the defining caution with agomelatine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hepatotoxicity. This is its key concern and mandates LFT monitoring before and during treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should LFTs be used when starting and continuing agomelatine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Check LFTs at baseline and at intervals during treatment (and on each dose increase). Do NOT start if transaminases are >3x the upper limit of normal, and STOP the drug if they rise to >3x the upper limit of normal.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When is agomelatine taken, and in which patients is it contraindicated or used with caution?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Taken at night (nocte). Contraindicated/used with caution in hepatic impairment because of its hepatotoxicity risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is trazodone markedly sedating, and what is its main practical use?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It blocks histamine and alpha-1 receptors, making it markedly sedating. It is used for depression with insomnia/agitation, and often LOW-DOSE for insomnia, especially in the elderly or for agitation in dementia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on trazodone develops a painful erection lasting several hours. What is this, and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Priapism - the classic exam adverse effect of trazodone. An erection lasting >4 hours is a urological emergency requiring immediate assessment. It results from alpha-1 blockade.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides priapism and sedation, what two cardiovascular/cardiac adverse effects should you watch for with trazodone?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Postural (orthostatic) hypotension - from alpha-1 blockade, causing dizziness and falls risk (important in the elderly) - and QT prolongation. Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging or serotonergic drugs and with MAOIs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do typical (first-generation) antipsychotics like haloperidol and chlorpromazine work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Potent D2 dopamine receptor blockade. Blocking the mesolimbic pathway gives the antipsychotic effect, but blockade of the other dopamine pathways causes extrapyramidal side effects (nigrostriatal) and raised prolactin (tuberoinfundibular).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Compared with atypicals, what is the main disadvantage of typical antipsychotics?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A higher risk of extrapyramidal side effects (dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) and hyperprolactinaemia, because of their strong D2 blockade.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main clinical uses of typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Schizophrenia/psychosis, acute agitation or delirium (haloperidol), and mania. Depot forms are used to support adherence. Levomepromazine is also used for antiemesis/hiccups in palliative care.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Name the four extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotics and their timing.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acute dystonia (within hours), akathisia (restlessness), parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia (late-onset and often irreversible).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on haloperidol develops an acute oculogyric crisis (eyes forced upward) and neck spasm. What is this and how is it treated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acute dystonia, an early extrapyramidal reaction occurring within hours. Treat with an anticholinergic such as procyclidine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is tardive dyskinesia and why does it matter?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A late-onset extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotics, typically involuntary repetitive facial/mouth movements. It appears after prolonged treatment and is often irreversible, so watch for it on long-term therapy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is akathisia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotics causing an unpleasant inner restlessness and inability to keep still. It can be mistaken for worsening agitation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does hyperprolactinaemia from antipsychotics present?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, and — long-term — osteoporosis from low sex hormone levels.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides EPSEs and raised prolactin, list the other important adverse effects of typical antipsychotics.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: QT prolongation, sedation, a lowered seizure threshold, increased VTE risk, postural/antimuscarinic effects, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should antipsychotics generally be avoided in Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Their dopamine blockade worsens motor symptoms, and patients with Lewy body dementia can have severe, sometimes life-threatening sensitivity reactions to antipsychotics.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are antipsychotics avoided in elderly patients with dementia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: All antipsychotics increase the risk of stroke and death in elderly people with dementia, so they are avoided or used only short-term when essential.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which QT-related precaution applies when prescribing haloperidol or other antipsychotics?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They prolong the QT interval. Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. certain antiarrhythmics, macrolides, ondansetron, methadone) and correct low potassium and magnesium. Check an ECG.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on an antipsychotic develops high fever, muscle rigidity, confusion, and unstable blood pressure/heart rate. What is the diagnosis?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — fever, rigidity, altered mental state, and autonomic instability, with a raised creatine kinase (CK).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is neuroleptic malignant syndrome managed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Stop the antipsychotic immediately and give supportive care with cooling and fluids. Dantrolene or bromocriptine may be used in severe cases. A raised creatine kinase supports the diagnosis.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What physical-health monitoring bundle applies to all antipsychotics?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weight/BMI, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, blood pressure, and an ECG (QT) — at baseline, 12 weeks, 1 year, then annually.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When is clozapine indicated in schizophrenia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: For treatment-resistant schizophrenia — after at least two other antipsychotics (each at an adequate dose for at least 6 weeks, one being a non-clozapine atypical) have failed. It is the most effective agent and also reduces suicidality.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is clozapine not used first-line despite being the most effective antipsychotic?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It has a serious toxicity profile (agranulocytosis, myocarditis, life-threatening constipation) requiring mandatory monitoring, so it is reserved for treatment-resistant disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What haematological adverse effect makes clozapine's blood monitoring mandatory, and what is the rule?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Agranulocytosis/neutropenia. Regular FBC monitoring is mandatory — 'no blood, no drug.' If neutrophils fall, stop clozapine and do not rechallenge.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the FBC monitoring schedule for clozapine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weekly for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly up to 1 year, then 4-weekly. The patient, prescriber, and pharmacy must be registered with a monitoring scheme.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient started on clozapine 6 weeks ago develops chest pain, breathlessness, and a fast heart rate. What must you suspect?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Myocarditis (or cardiomyopathy) — a serious clozapine toxicity with highest risk in the first 2 months. Check ECG/troponin and stop the drug if suspected.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is constipation a serious safety issue with clozapine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Clozapine can cause severe constipation progressing to life-threatening bowel obstruction/ileus (an MHRA warning). Ask about bowel function regularly and treat constipation promptly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does smoking affect clozapine levels, and why does this matter?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Smoking lowers clozapine levels, so stopping smoking raises levels and can cause toxicity. The dose may need adjusting when a patient's smoking status changes.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A clozapine patient has missed all doses for more than 48 hours. Can they simply restart their usual dose?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No. If more than 48 hours of doses are missed, clozapine must be re-titrated from a low dose, because restarting the full dose abruptly risks toxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Name two clozapine side effects other than agranulocytosis, myocarditis, and constipation.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Paradoxical hypersalivation, marked weight gain/diabetes, sedation, a dose-related lowered seizure threshold, and increased VTE risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does clozapine cause few extrapyramidal side effects and little prolactin rise?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It has relatively weak D2 blockade (with rapid dissociation from the receptor), so it produces very low EPSE and prolactin compared with other antipsychotics.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the defining adverse effect of olanzapine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A high metabolic burden — marked weight gain, dyslipidaemia, and diabetes/impaired glucose tolerance (metabolic syndrome). It is the worst antipsychotic for metabolic effects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is olanzapine's advantage over typical antipsychotics, and its main downside in practice?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an effective atypical with low EPSE, but it is very sedating and has the worst metabolic profile (weight gain, diabetes, raised lipids).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which monitoring is especially important for a patient on olanzapine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weight/BMI, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipids at baseline and regularly, because of its high risk of weight gain and diabetes.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must IM olanzapine not be combined with an IM benzodiazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The combination risks serious cardiorespiratory depression. They should not be given together for rapid tranquillisation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does risperidone differ from other atypical antipsychotics in its side-effect profile?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: At higher doses it has relatively strong D2 blockade, giving more dose-related extrapyramidal side effects and the highest prolactin rise of the atypicals.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which antipsychotic is the only one licensed for persistent aggression in Alzheimer's dementia, and with what limit?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Risperidone — licensed short-term only, for a maximum of 6 weeks, because of the stroke and mortality risk of antipsychotics in dementia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia should you watch for in a patient on risperidone?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, and long-term osteoporosis — risperidone causes the most prolactin elevation of the atypicals, so check prolactin at baseline and if symptomatic.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What administration option makes risperidone or paliperidone useful for patients with poor adherence?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A long-acting depot (long-acting injection), which maintains treatment without daily oral dosing.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: By what mechanism does quetiapine achieve very low rates of extrapyramidal side effects and low prolactin despite being a dopamine blocker?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It binds the dopamine (D2) receptor but dissociates rapidly ('hit-and-run'), so it does not occupy the receptor long enough to cause significant EPSE or a sustained rise in prolactin.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient started on quetiapine complains of marked drowsiness and feeling faint on standing. Which receptor-blocking effects explain this?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Strong histamine (H1) blockade causes sedation, and alpha-adrenergic blockade causes postural (orthostatic) hypotension. These are quetiapine's characteristic early tolerability problems.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Across which phases of bipolar disorder can quetiapine be used?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: All of them — acute mania, bipolar depression, and long-term maintenance. Being effective in bipolar depression (as well as schizophrenia) is a key selling point of quetiapine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is quetiapine sometimes prescribed at low dose off-label, and is this a licensed use?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Low-dose quetiapine is used off-label for sleep and agitation, exploiting its sedating (H1) effect. This is not a licensed indication and should be recognised as off-label prescribing.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do quetiapine's metabolic side effects and EPSE/prolactin profile compare with other atypicals?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Moderate metabolic effects (weight gain, glucose/lipid changes) but less than olanzapine, together with very low EPSE and low prolactin. It also prolongs the QT interval.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring and caution apply to quetiapine in a patient with cardiac disease or on other QT-prolonging drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Quetiapine prolongs the QT interval, so avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs and obtain an ECG if there is cardiac risk. Also run the metabolic bundle (weight, glucose, lipids).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of aripiprazole, and what nickname reflects it?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a dopamine (D2) partial agonist — a 'dopamine system stabiliser'. Rather than fully blocking D2, it partially activates it, dampening excess dopamine while providing some tone where dopamine is low.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is aripiprazole often chosen when metabolic side effects, sedation, or high prolactin must be minimised?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As a D2 partial agonist it causes the least weight gain/metabolic disturbance, the least prolactin rise (it can even lower prolactin), and the least sedation of the common atypicals.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on aripiprazole reports inner restlessness, an inability to sit still, and trouble sleeping. What are these characteristic effects?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Akathisia (restlessness) and insomnia/activation are aripiprazole's signature adverse effects, reflecting its activating, partial-agonist profile rather than sedation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What impulse-control problems has the MHRA warned can occur with aripiprazole, and what should you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping, and binge eating. Ask about these directly, warn patients, and consider dose reduction or stopping if they emerge.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which atypical antipsychotic can actually lower prolactin, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Aripiprazole — because it is a dopamine (D2) partial agonist rather than a full blocker, dopamine tone at the pituitary is preserved, so prolactin stays low or falls.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of amisulpride?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A relatively selective dopamine D2/D3 antagonist with negligible serotonin (5-HT2A) activity. At low dose it blocks presynaptic autoreceptors, raising dopamine release and helping negative symptoms.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is low-dose amisulpride useful for the negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: At low dose it preferentially blocks presynaptic autoreceptors, which increases dopamine release. This boosts dopamine signalling and improves negative symptoms; higher doses block postsynaptic receptors for positive/psychotic symptoms.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which two adverse effects is amisulpride particularly notorious for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Marked hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, long-term osteoporosis) and QT prolongation. It also causes dose-related EPSE and insomnia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is amisulpride eliminated, and what practical implication does this have?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is largely renally excreted, so the dose must be reduced (or the drug avoided) in renal impairment. Check renal function before and during treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What must be checked and corrected before and during amisulpride treatment because of its QT effect?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Baseline and on-treatment ECG for the QT interval, and correct low potassium or magnesium first. Avoid co-prescribing other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which newer atypical is licensed for bipolar depression and must be taken with food?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lurasidone — it is used in schizophrenia and bipolar depression, and must be taken with a meal of at least ~350 kcal, because food is needed for adequate absorption.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are lurasidone and cariprazine chosen over older atypicals in patients where weight gain is a concern?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Both are metabolically favourable, causing little weight gain and minimal metabolic disturbance. This tolerability advantage is the main reason to select them.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of cariprazine and what is it particularly useful for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a dopamine partial agonist with a preference for the D3 receptor. This makes it useful for the negative symptoms of schizophrenia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the main shared adverse effect of lurasidone and cariprazine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Akathisia (and other EPSE), along with nausea. Despite being metabolically favourable, their key tolerability issue is restlessness/EPSE rather than weight gain.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What key interactions must you check before prescribing lurasidone?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is contraindicated with strong metabolic enzyme inhibitors and inducers, and grapefruit should be avoided — these change lurasidone levels significantly. Examples include clarithromycin, rifampicin, and grapefruit juice.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which atypical antipsychotics are the most metabolically favourable, and which cause the most weight gain?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Most favourable: aripiprazole, lurasidone, and cariprazine (little weight gain). Worst for weight gain/metabolic effects: olanzapine and clozapine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which atypicals cause the greatest rise in prolactin, and which cause the least?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Greatest prolactin rise: risperidone and amisulpride. Least: aripiprazole (can even lower it) and quetiapine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: For a patient with schizophrenia who is very concerned about weight gain and sedation, which atypical is a logical choice and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Aripiprazole — as a D2 partial agonist it has the least weight gain/metabolic effect, least prolactin rise, and least sedation. Counsel about possible akathisia, activation/insomnia, and impulse-control problems.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which mood stabiliser is first-line for long-term prophylaxis in bipolar disorder?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lithium. It prevents both manic and depressive relapse and has the best evidence for reducing suicide risk. It is also used to augment antidepressants in resistant depression.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the target serum lithium level for maintenance, and why is monitoring essential?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: 0.4-1.0 mmol/L, aiming ~0.6-0.8 mmol/L. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, so levels only slightly above range cause toxicity - regular level checks are mandatory.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When after a dose should a lithium level be taken, and how often?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: 12 hours post-dose. Check weekly until stable, then every 3 months once the dose is established.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why do dehydration and a low-salt state raise lithium levels?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lithium is handled by the kidney like sodium and reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. When the body conserves sodium (dehydration/low salt), it also retains lithium, pushing levels up towards toxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Name three classes of drug that raise lithium levels and can precipitate toxicity.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and thiazide diuretics. All reduce lithium excretion. Dehydration and a low-sodium diet do the same - counsel patients accordingly and avoid NSAIDs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on lithium develops a coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, vomiting and confusion. What is happening?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lithium toxicity. Features progress from coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and GI upset to confusion, and if severe to seizures and coma.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is lithium toxicity managed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Stop lithium, give IV fluids (0.9% saline) to rehydrate and restore sodium, and use haemodialysis if levels are very high or the patient is severely symptomatic.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does the tremor of stable lithium therapy differ from that of toxicity?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Therapeutic lithium causes a benign fine tremor. A new coarse tremor is a red flag for toxicity and should prompt an urgent level check.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does long-term lithium cause polyuria and polydipsia?
