pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus - the kidney becomes insensitive to ADH, so it cannot concentrate urine. This gives dilute polyuria and compensatory thirst.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which endocrine glands are affected by long-term lithium?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The thyroid (hypothyroidism and goitre) and the parathyroids (hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia). This is why thyroid function and calcium are monitored.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What renal harm can chronic lithium cause besides diabetes insipidus?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Chronic kidney impairment (a progressive decline in renal function). Renal function must be checked before starting and monitored during treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is lithium avoided in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is teratogenic, classically causing Ebstein's anomaly (a cardiac defect). It is contraindicated/avoided in pregnancy and in those planning to conceive.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What must you check before starting lithium, and what is monitored long-term?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Check renal and thyroid function before starting. Long-term, monitor lithium levels plus U&Es, thyroid function and calcium roughly every 6 months.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should lithium always be prescribed by a consistent brand?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Different preparations have differing bioavailability, so switching brand can change the serum level and risk toxicity or loss of effect. Patients also receive the lithium information pack (purple booklet and alert card).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the role of valproate in bipolar disorder?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an anti-manic mood stabiliser used for acute mania and maintenance (an antipsychotic is usually first-line for acute mania). It is also an antiepileptic for generalised and absence seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is valproate so strongly restricted in people of childbearing potential?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is highly teratogenic, causing neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental disorders. It must not be used in anyone of childbearing potential except under a Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What does the valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme require?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Effective contraception, annual review by a specialist, and a signed Risk Acknowledgement Form confirming the patient understands the risks in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What did the MHRA 2024 advice change about starting valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It must not be started in any new patient under 55 (either sex) unless two independent specialists agree there is no suitable alternative. Men face fertility and offspring risks, so the restriction applies to both sexes.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which two common cosmetic side effects should you warn a patient starting valproate about?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weight gain and hair loss - the hair typically regrows curly. A fine tremor is also common.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which serious organ toxicities can valproate cause?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis. LFTs are checked before starting and during the first 6 months, and pancreatitis should be considered in a patient with abdominal pain and vomiting.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What haematological side effect of valproate is monitored with an FBC?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count). FBC is checked as part of monitoring alongside LFTs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on valproate becomes drowsy and confused but their LFTs are normal - what should you consider?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy. Valproate can raise ammonia and cause encephalopathy even when LFTs are normal - check an ammonia level.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What happens to lamotrigine levels when valproate is co-prescribed, and what must you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Valproate is an enzyme inhibitor and raises lamotrigine levels, increasing the risk of serious rash. The lamotrigine dose must be halved.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should carbapenem antibiotics be avoided in a patient on valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbapenems dramatically lower valproate levels, risking loss of seizure or mood control. The combination should be avoided.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which pole of bipolar disorder is lamotrigine particularly useful for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The depressive pole - it is a mood stabiliser best for preventing bipolar depression. It is weight-neutral, well tolerated, and a safer option than valproate in women of childbearing age.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the most dangerous adverse effect of lamotrigine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A serious rash - Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or DRESS. Any rash should prompt stopping the drug.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is lamotrigine dosed to reduce the risk of a serious rash?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Start low and titrate slowly - rapid dose escalation is a major risk factor for Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN. Patients are told to report any rash immediately.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is the lamotrigine dose halved when combined with valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Valproate raises lamotrigine levels, which increases the risk of a serious rash. Halving the dose offsets this interaction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What effect do enzyme inducers and the combined oral contraceptive have on lamotrigine levels?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Both lower lamotrigine levels. With the combined pill, levels fall during active pills and rise again in the pill-free week, which can affect seizure/mood control.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbamazepine, a sodium-channel blocker. It is also used for focal epilepsy and, on a specialist basis only, for bipolar disorder.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why can carbamazepine cause contraceptive failure?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a potent enzyme inducer that lowers levels of many drugs including hormonal contraceptives. Women need a reliable non-affected contraceptive method; it also reduces the effect of warfarin, DOACs and other antiepileptics.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is 'auto-induction' with carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbamazepine induces its own metabolism, so clearance rises over the first weeks of treatment. It is started low and titrated up to account for this.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What electrolyte disturbance does carbamazepine cause, and how does this contrast with lithium?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyponatraemia (an SIADH-like effect). This is the opposite of lithium, which causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Sodium is monitored via U&Es.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which haematological and skin reactions should prompt caution with carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Blood dyscrasias (leucopenia, aplastic anaemia) and serious rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN. Warn patients to report rash, fever or bruising, and monitor FBC.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which patients should be screened for HLA-B*1502 before starting carbamazepine, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Patients of South-East Asian ancestry. Carrying HLA-B*1502 markedly increases the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN with carbamazepine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring is required for a patient on carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: FBC (blood dyscrasias), U&Es for sodium (hyponatraemia), and LFTs (hepatotoxicity). It is also teratogenic, causing neural tube defects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do benzodiazepines act at the GABA-A receptor at the level of the chloride channel?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They bind an allosteric site on the GABA-A receptor and increase the FREQUENCY of chloride channel opening (they need endogenous GABA to work). This enhances GABA-mediated inhibition -> sedation, anxiolysis, muscle relaxation and anticonvulsant effects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are benzodiazepines safer than barbiturates in overdose?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Benzodiazepines require endogenous GABA to act (they increase the frequency of channel opening), which gives a ceiling effect. Barbiturates increase the duration of channel opening and can act without GABA, so they have no ceiling and are far more dangerous in overdose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should benzodiazepines only be used short-term (about 2-4 weeks)?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Regular use causes tolerance and dependence. They are therefore for short-term crises only and are NOT appropriate for routine treatment of generalised anxiety or insomnia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main clinical indications for benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Status epilepticus/seizures, alcohol withdrawal, acute agitation and procedural sedation, and muscle spasm - all short-term. They are not for routine long-term anxiety or insomnia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which benzodiazepines are used for status epilepticus/acute seizures, and by what route?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: IV lorazepam (in hospital), buccal midazolam, or rectal diazepam (useful in the community/children).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which drugs are used for alcohol withdrawal, and why is a benzodiazepine appropriate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Chlordiazepoxide or diazepam. Alcohol acts on GABA, so a benzodiazepine substitutes and is tapered down, preventing withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is diazepam a poor choice in the elderly or in liver disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Diazepam is long-acting because it has an active metabolite that accumulates, prolonging sedation and increasing falls/confusion risk. This accumulation is worse in the elderly and in hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which benzodiazepines are preferred in liver disease and the elderly, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The 'LOT' drugs - Lorazepam, Oxazepam and Temazepam. They have no active metabolite, so they do not accumulate and are safer where clearance is impaired.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the key side effects of benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation and drowsiness, falls (especially the elderly), anterograde amnesia, respiratory depression, and paradoxical agitation. Tolerance and dependence develop with regular use.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on regular benzodiazepines stops them abruptly. What is the danger and how should they be stopped?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium due to rebound hyperexcitability. Benzodiazepines must be tapered slowly, not stopped suddenly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is co-prescribing a benzodiazepine with an opioid dangerous?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: There is additive CNS depression -> profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death (MHRA warning). Avoid the combination or use the lowest possible doses with close monitoring.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose and what is the caution with its use?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Flumazenil (a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist). Use cautiously - in a dependent patient it can precipitate seizures, and its short duration may mean re-sedation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which conditions are benzodiazepines contraindicated or used with great caution?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Respiratory depression, severe respiratory disease and sleep apnoea; myasthenia gravis; and severe hepatic impairment. Caution in the elderly due to falls and confusion.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do Z-drugs (zopiclone, zolpidem, zaleplon) work, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They act at the same benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor but are hypnotic-selective, so they promote sleep with less anxiolytic/muscle-relaxant effect. They carry the same dependence risk as benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the correct place in therapy for Z-drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Short-term insomnia only (about 2-4 weeks), after sleep hygiene and CBT for insomnia have been tried. They are not used for anxiety, and there is no clear advantage over short-acting benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which Z-drug classically causes a bitter/metallic taste?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Zopiclone.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the key safety concerns with Z-drugs in practice?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Next-day driving impairment (especially zopiclone/higher-dose zolpidem), falls in the elderly, dependence/tolerance, rebound insomnia on stopping, and complex sleep behaviours.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on zolpidem reports episodes of sleep-walking and sleep-driving. What must be done?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Stop the Z-drug permanently (MHRA advice on complex sleep behaviours). Warn patients to avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants which increase the risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does buspirone produce anxiolysis, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist that works without any action on GABA. So it causes no sedation, no dependence and no muscle relaxation - unlike benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is buspirone used for and why is it useless for acute or PRN anxiety?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is used for generalised anxiety disorder. It takes about 2 weeks to work and must be taken regularly, so it is ineffective for acute or as-needed anxiety relief.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What advice about food/drink and other drugs should you give with buspirone?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Avoid grapefruit (it can raise buspirone levels - levels also rise with certain enzyme inhibitors). Avoid MAOIs (risk of hypertension) and use caution with other serotonergic drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the main advantage of buspirone over benzodiazepines for anxiety?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No dependence and no sedation. The trade-off is slow onset (about 2 weeks) and the need for regular dosing.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What type of drug is hydroxyzine and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A sedating antihistamine (H1 antagonist) with anxiolytic and antipruritic effects. It is used for short-term anxiety and for pruritus/urticaria, and is non-dependence-forming.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key cardiac safety concern with hydroxyzine, and what are the dose limits?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: QT prolongation. To limit this (MHRA), the maximum is 100 mg/day in adults and 50 mg/day in the elderly. Avoid in patients with a long QT or on other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides QT prolongation, what side effects limit hydroxyzine use, especially in the elderly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation and antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, worsening glaucoma). Use caution in the elderly and in prostatism/glaucoma.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do pregabalin and gabapentin work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. This gives anxiolytic, anticonvulsant and neuropathic-pain effects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main indications for pregabalin/gabapentin, and where does pregabalin sit for GAD?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Neuropathic pain (e.g. diabetic, post-herpetic), adjunct in focal epilepsy, and generalised anxiety disorder. For GAD, pregabalin is third-line, after an SSRI then an SNRI.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are prescriptions of pregabalin and gabapentin now more tightly controlled?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are controlled drugs because of misuse, diversion and dependence potential. They can also produce euphoria.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should pregabalin/gabapentin dosing be adjusted in renal impairment, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The dose must be reduced because they are renally cleared, so they accumulate if renal function is poor - increasing sedation and respiratory-depression risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the notable side effects of pregabalin/gabapentin?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation, dizziness, weight gain and peripheral oedema. Pregabalin also carries a signal for congenital malformations in pregnancy (MHRA).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is combining a gabapentinoid with an opioid dangerous?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Additive CNS/respiratory depression can cause serious respiratory depression (MHRA warning), particularly in the elderly and those with renal or respiratory disease. The same caution applies with alcohol and benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does propranolol help anxiety, and what symptom does it NOT treat?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks the physical/somatic adrenergic symptoms of anxiety - tremor, palpitations, tachycardia and sweating. It does not treat the psychological component.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: For which type of anxiety is propranolol most useful, and how is it dosed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Situational/performance anxiety (e.g. exams, public speaking), where somatic symptoms dominate. It is given as 10-40 mg, taken PRN before the stressor (or regularly). It causes no dependence.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must propranolol be avoided in asthma, and what other caution applies in diabetes?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Being non-selective, it can cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. In diabetes it can mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia (e.g. tremor, tachycardia).
